description: Additional ciphers which appear to be written by a different hand and quill and added to the manuscript at a later date. These folios were probably written by Dr W. Wynn Westcott. a; Union tablet of the Elemental Tables. With handwritten note on reverse in Westcott’s hand stating ‘Union Tablet of the Elemental Tables’. [GD 1/1/8a] b; 5° = 6° [Adeptus Minor] Opening Ceremony, which is the first grade of the Second or Inner Order of the R. R. et A. C. [Ordo Rosae Rubeae et Aureae Crucis] With two handwritten annotations by Dr Westcott at the top of the front stating ‘5° = 6° Opening Ceremony ([paper] circa 1790 says the British Museum authorities.)’ and the word ‘Curious’ within the text. Folio translates into French and Latin. [GD 1/1/8b] c; Gives the name and address of Fräulein Sprengel, with handwritten note by Dr Westcott within text stating ‘who lived there often’. [GD 1/1/8c]

description: Cipher manuscript written on paper, in brown ink. Most folios do not form part of the original cipher but give additional information on the grades. Creator unknown [thought to have been written by Frank William Colman, Praemonstrator and Hiereus of the Osiris Temple]. a; The opening of the Zelator Ceremony Annotated on reverse in pencil ‘1=10 GD Ritual – Crux dat Salutem’ [Motto of Benjamin Cox, Imperator and Hierophant of the Osiris Temple, Weston-super-Mare]. [GD1/2/3a] b,Describes the admission badges for each grade. Annotated on reverse in pencil ‘Coleman’s modern copy of admission Badges of each grade from our information’. [GD1/2/3b]. c; Annotated on reverse in pencil ‘Insignia Clothing of G D in the Outer Coleman’. [GD1/2/3c]. d; Cipher depicting a pentagram. Annotated on reverse ‘G D scheme applied to the Pentagram Coleman’ [GD1/2/3d]. e; Annotated on reverse ‘Luna on the Tree Coleman [from ?]‘ [GD1/2/3e]. f; Annotated on reverse 'about the Paths between the grades Coleman’ [GD1/2/3f]. g; Annotated on reverse ‘Elementals of the 4 grades, grades necessary to officers of Temples, names of grades’[GD1/2/3g]. h; Annotated on reverse ‘Summary 4 grades of [lowest] order of the G D in the outer Coleman’ [GD1/2/3h]
title: Copies of the cipher manuscript and later additional ciphers by [Frank William Colman]

Acknowledges letter from Constantinople, cover given in cipher, but has not yet received a promised 'long' letter via Ragusa. - Explains the purpose of his mission to Saxony. - Refers to his, Paget's, brother's stay at Vienna: he has conveyed to him Paget's request for the withdrawal of his [first] receipt for extraordinaries. Gives him the latest European news: the duke of Savoy has lost the battle at Marsaglia in which Charles Schomberg [second duke of Schomberg] was fatally wounded. The duke of Leinster is his heir. Compares the duke of Savoy to 'a tree which takes root deeper the more it is shaken'. Yet the imperial court seems 'a little uneasy' about his future steadfastness in the face of lack of succour, England and the States being the only hope, '& on the other side the Pope and the French king renew their instances towards reconciling his royal highness who, when he finds himself abandoned, may comply out of despair.'. The 'storm' of Ratzeburg is 'well over'. - The King has landed at Harwich on Oct 29/Nov 8 and was to meet parliament on Nov 7/17. The States have resolved to increase their forces by 15,000 men. - The English admirals 'are making warre ashore' and quarreling with Falkland, first lord of the admiralty who 'in all appearances will have the better of them'. - Hopes to hear soon 'at whose door the fault[s] and blunders of our sea affairs will be layd'. Date and Place: 1693 Nov 17/27 Dresden.

context: The Security Service: Personal (PF Series) Files. WORLD WAR II. German Intelligence Agents and Suspected Agents.
description: Tyler KENT: American. KENT, a cipher clerk at the US Embassy in London, was detained in May 1940 on suspicion of improperly providing information derived from his employment to Anna WOLKOFF an active member of the Right Club in correspondence with the renegade William JOYCE [''Lord Haw Haw''] and in contact with Italian diplomats in London; and to Captain Maule RAMSAY MP, founder of the Right Club. Kent's diplomatic immunity was withdrawn by Ambassador Kennedy and a search of his flat revealed a mass of copied classified material together with the membership records of the Right Club which had been given to Kent for safe keeping. Kent was tried on five charges under Section 1 of the Official Secrets Act and two under the Larceny Act in October 1940 and sentenced to seven years' imprisonment. On his release in November 1945 he was deported to the USA.

KENT was tried on five charges under Section 1 of the Official Secrets Act and two under the Larceny Act 1916 in October 1940 and sentenced to seven years' imprisonment. On his release in November 1945 he was deported to the USA.

note: Numerous passages and sentences in both main letter and postscript underlined and glossed by Stepney.
description: Folio 113. From Colt. Acknowledges letter of Feb 8/18. Has examined the cipher 'which answeres every word'. The things of which Stepney cautions him 'are very publick here' [i.e. at Dresden, referring, probably, to the Elector's association with the countess Rochlitz] as he noticed on his arrival. He will 'take care' of the person mentioned by Stepney, namely Haxthausen ['Haxhuysen', interlinear gloss by Stepney] who has already given him evidence of deserving the character given him by Stepney. Has made his 'court' to the countess Platen ['to countesse of Platten', interlinear gloss by Stepney]. Thinks he had some share in the Elector's favour: the prince gave him a bracelet from his wrist, telling him 'it was not an order but a marke of his friendship' and that the inscription on one side 'uni pour jamais' was designed for my master and 'amitié sincere'.. was for myself'. Thinks he is being treated with 'great distinction'; has not 'heard one disrespectful word spoken of our master concerning Schöning which was very frequent before my arrival'. - Heeckeren has warned him that his colleagues of the diplomatic corps suspect him of pleading for Schöning, that the Elector had said he, Colt, had given him 'hopes of Schöning's liberty' and that he had talked in the same vein to the 'prisoner's wife'. When he pressed to know the 'author' of the story, the Brandenburg envoy [Chwalkowski] told him that the prince of Anhalt[-Dessau, John George II] had written him 'asking for the truth'. He told his fellow envoys that, like the rest of them, he had visited the lady, but only to persuade her to 'imploy her creditt with the Elector to comply with the Emperor as the only way to save her husband's life and honour'; of this he notified Sternberg. Adds that there was much malice and places it 'on one that should treat me better' ['van Heckeren', interlinear gloss by Stepney]. None the less, Schöning's family do not let it rest there. They purport to have letters from Vienna according to which Sternberg has instructions different from those he 'owns' and that the Emperor 'would comply rather than these [i.e. Saxon] troops should stay at home'. - Has now 'complyed to sign' for 150,000 Rixdollars, but 'my compagnion' ['Heckeren', interlinear gloss by Stepney], who alone has orders, wishes him to pay 100,000 on account, the rest later. Complains of being under pressure [by Heeckeren], yet left without express instructions, but will 'never yield' to signing, as Heeckeren argues with him, for a certain present to a minister, 'as shall be necessary' [Four words in cipher: two thereof, '1101: 104', glossed by Stepney 'Minister S'. As for countess Rochlitz, see SP 105/82, ff.156, 170, 172 and 174(PS.)]. Is also in ignorance, as are his 'comrades' Heeckeren and Ilten [Heckeren and Ilten' interlinear gloss by Stepney] of the reinforcements treaty with Denmark about to be concluded, when, at the same time, he has to explain to Sternberg that it will not be prejudicial to the Emperor or the allies. - Reference to the arrival of a new envoy from Hessen-Cassel [Frederick baron Kettler] who has signed with other princes at Ratisbon and declared the 'third party' as 'ruinous to the Empire'. He will join his troops to the Elector's in the next campaign. PS.: by Schweinfurt. The Elector has now fully resolved to march with his troops though he has had no satisfaction from the Emperor concerning Schöning. The Saxon ministers are now with Sternberg 'adjusting the treaty' and Colt is to confer with Heeckeren about a modus to pay their part of the sum as promised. Grote is to leave for Vienna [on special mission] within the next few days. Schweinfurt will send Stepney any papers he may require through [George Michael] Bacmeister [Grote's secretary]. Acknowledges letter of Feb 11/21. Date and Place: 1693 Feb 17/27 Dresden.

title: Letter from Mr Smith [Lord Hatton], Paris, to Sir Edward Nicholas. Received 5 Sep. He apologizes for his silence and laments his troubles; he warns against the Scots; he has heard that the emperor is deterred from helping the King because of the 'civil wars' in the latter's court; news of the new Venetian ambassador to France; the agreement between France and the Princes of Italy against Spain; Downing's embassy to Savoy has been diverted to Paris; the Genevan resident has told Hatton of the designs of the Huguenots; his fears for the state of the royalist cause in England and the impact to the divisions in the court in Cologne. Original letter, without wrapper; some sentences and names in cipher, deciphered in hand of Nicholas, who also writes endorsement. 4pp

title: Letter from Sir Richard Browne, Paris, to Sir Edward Nicholas: he regrets the breach between Charles II and the Duke of York; he does not know why the English ships were seized in Marseilles but suspects the Duke of Vendome; the cardinal has gout but has intervened to protect Monsieur Augiers who has killed a crochetteur; the French clergy will vote a contribution; Queen Christina's presence in north Germany is not welcome; the French, with Cromwell's connivance, will attempt to hinder Dutch trade with Spain; some secret instructions for the French ambassador in England have been captured and taken to Flanders. Original letter; a few words in cipher, deciphered in hand of EN, whose rough hand writes the endorsement. 2pp Numbered 13 [Not printed by Bray among Sir Richard Browne's letters in vol IV of his edition of Evelyn's Diary]

note: Ayton’s transcript of the Cipher Manuscript is the earliest known copy. It was from this copy that a plate of the manuscript included in Waite’s Brotherhood of the Rosy Cross was taken.
physicalCondition: Bound, quarto volume, covered in vellum
description: Volume contains Instructional material for the Adeptus Minor Grade, written in the hand of the Rev William A. Ayton. With finely executed line diagrams and colour illustrations of the elemental weapons and watercolour drawing of an angelic figure. [see p.121] Volume also includes a transcript of the cipher manuscript by Ayton. [GD 1/1] This transcript includes the opening of the 1=10 Zelator Ceremony which is now not extant in the original cipher manuscript. context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Scotland Series I, Mary Queen of Scots.
adminHistory: At the time of the Babington plot against Elizabeth I in 1586, the cipher letters passed through government hands and were deciphered by Sir Francis Walsingham's factotum, Thomas Phelippes, but before his time deciphering was the work of John Somers, clerk of the signet.
description: A special collection of documents (some transferred from SP 59) particularly concerning Mary, Queen of Scots from her flight from Scotland into England in 1568 until her execution in 1587. Thus the records span only part of Elizabeth I's reign. The series contains correspondence between the Queen Mary and Queen Elizabeth, their ministers and representatives, not least Mary's custodian's evidence of Mary's and her supporters' machinations, including her 'casket letters' to the Earl of Bothwell, her third husband, and, above all, the papers seized at Chartley Castle on the discovery of the Babington conspiracy in 1586 which were used, when deciphered, to implicate Mary and bring her to trial. The series includes a collection of over 100 ciphers, most of them used in communication with Mary. and used to decipher calendared letters. Different ciphers were used by the Queen's correspondents. Some of these correspondents are identified, but some remain 'anonymous'.
title: Secretaries of State: State Papers Scotland Series I, Mary Queen of Scots

description: Letter of Aleister Crowley, 49 rue Vavin, Montparnasse, Paris to W[illiam] Wynn Westcott, 396 Camden Road, London, reporting that the writer has received letters from [Arthur] Cadbury Jones sent on behalf of Westcott but does not believe that the matters in question can be settled by a third party; asks Westcott about the Cipher MSS, on which the Rosaie Rubeae et Aurex Crucis and Golden Dawn were founded; says they are being exploited by swindlers such as Madame Horos; accuses Westcott of being their accomplice by clocking access to the Cipher MSS; believes Cipher MSS contain hidden formulae of initiation into the Golden Dawn; determined to vindicate their veracity on behalf of initiates as the guardian of the Order; demands Westcott makes a clear statement about how he obtained the Cipher MSS, which should be deposited at the British Museum or must inform Crowley to whom he has entrusted them; wishes to authenticate the Cipher MSS and to share the knowledge with genuine students; threatens to publish a complete statement about the transaction from the time of Sapiens Dominabitur Astris [motto of Fräulein Sprengel]to the present day but offers Westcott an opportunity to state his own case given the accusation of forgery by his colleague [Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers]; if Westcott finds this course of action displeasing then it is his own fault as Crowley aims to play fair; should Non Omnis Moriar [motto of Dr W Wynn Westcott] consider that Crowley writes without proper authority, the writer has had this letter supervised and approved by V.V.V.V.V. [motto of Aleister Crowley] of the Argenteum Astrum; D.D.S. [motto unknown] and O.M. [motto unknown]. The letter includes silver wax seal impressions of Aleister Crowley with eye Hieroglyph and black waxseal of O.M. [GD 3/4/1/11a]; envelope of On His Majesty's Service returned letter dated 14 August [GD 3/4/1/11b].
title: Letter of Aleister Crowley to W Wynn Westcott with envelope

context: Admiralty: Operational Intelligence Centre: Intelligence from Intercepted German, Italian and Japanese Radio Communications, WWII.
adminHistory: During the war of 1939-1945, radio messages transmitted by the German, Italian and Japanese armed forces were, whenever possible ciphered, intercepted by allied radio operators. Ciphered messages intercepted by British radio stations were decrypted at the Government Code and Cipher School at Bletchley Park in Buckinghamshire ('B.P' or 'Station X'), and then sent to the intelligence staffs of operational forces at home and overseas. The German armed forces made extensive use of an electrical keyboard (the Enigma machine) which produced an extremely complex and easily varied means of enciphering and deciphering signals; the system was thought to be secure for all practical purposes, and was in constant use for important communications throughout the war. Bletchley Park, however had an Enigma machine acquired just before the war, and further machines with current settings were captured from time to time. With the aid of these and of computers which they were developing independently, the British cryptanalysts were able to read a high proportion of enemy signals enciphered in this way. In order to preserve the secret that the cipher could be broken, intelligence derived from Enigma signals was given a special security classification, MSS (Most Secret Source) or Ultra, and disguised as having come from agents in enemy territory, or from prisoners of war.
arrangement: The files were bound in order of the German time of origin (in some cases upwards from the bottom of the file), irrespective of the time and date of decrypting, the cipher employed (which is rarely indicated), or the area, type of vessel, or significance of the signal. The copies that compose this series follow the same arrangement.
description: File copies of teleprinter messages. The various series of messages are of two distinct types: intercepted signals, decrypted, translated, and sent from the German Naval Section of the Admiralty's Naval Intelligence Division at Bletchley Park to the division's Operational Intelligence Centre in the Admiralty; and summaries of intelligence derived from such signals sent to the War Office, Air Ministry and overseas commands. These signals became known as ULTRA. Records within this series are available to download as digital microfilm.
title: Admiralty: Operational Intelligence Centre: Intelligence from Intercepted German, Italian and Japanese Radio Communications, WWII

context: Government Code and Cypher School: Air Section: Reports on Italian and Other Foreign Air Forces (AS/AS- Series).
arrangement: Reports in the AS series, which were based on decrypts of messages sent in the ciphers of a number of different national Air Forces, carry a unique serial number in the top right hand corner in the range 1-1899, immediately below which is the date the report was issued. This is followed by the reports title, the routing of the cipher message and the message text. For the most part, reports contain a single cipher message. The AS series was replaced in July 1940 by the ASI series, based solely on decrypts of Italian Air Force ciphers: these initially had the same format as the AS reports but gradually the titles and routings were dropped and by the end of May 1941, each with their own ASI number, were being sent out in batches. ASI numbers were allocated in the range 1-10000, at which they reverted to 1, the second series stopping as 7232, in 1943/1944; reports based on decrypts of these ciphers were issued in the AS(P) series, numbers 1-120. There is also a small AS(R) series dealing with the Russian Air Force, which will form part of a separate release of the Soviet material. The reports are arranged numerically in books/folders in the following sequence: AS series (April 1936-August 1940) Italian Air Force Orders of Battle Index to ASI series ASI 1-10000 (July 1940-July 1942) ASI 1-7232 (July 1942-November 1943) ASAA 1-3 XC/JC series CCC IRT 1-22 MERCHANT PK 1-660 ITAM series AS AS(P) For pieces described at item level, the items were numbered arbitarily prior to accessioning. These item numbers do not appear on the reports themselves.
description: Intelligence reports on foreign (European) air forces produced by the Air Section. To aid the understanding of these reports, a number of working aids and orders of Battle are also included, also some correspondence files relating to the reports. The reports are copies of teleprinted reports to Service Ministries on the activities primarily of the Italian Air Force, both before and during the Second World War. Information on pre-war activities include operations in Spain during the Spanish Civil War, also activity in North Africa, the Aegean and Ethiopia. Information on war time activities includes operations in Africa, the Aegean, Corsica, Sardinia, Sicily and mainland Italy, also operations in Russia. Information on other air force activities in reports comprises: the Spanish Air Forces (Nationalist and Insurgent) during the Spanish Civil War and the Spanish Air Forces subsequently between 1941 and 1945; some activity by the German Air Force in the Spanish Civil War and in and around Europe, prior to and in the early stages of the Second World War - operations by the German Air Forces in North Africa and the Mediterranean are to some extent covered by the Italian Air Force reporting; Russian operations in Finland in 1940; French activity in the Mediterranean, 1939-1943; Portuguese Air Force between August 1943 and October 1944 The reports describe combat operations, transport flights, accidents, deployments and other order of battle changes, readiness states of aircraft and air crews, fuel situations at individual airfields and attaché reports (those from the Italian Air Attaché in Tokyo described Japanese operations in the Far East). The reports are all based on decrypts of medium/low grade cipher messages: some are verbatim copies of translations while others are paraphrases of the original text.
title: Government Code and Cypher School: Air Section: Reports on Italian and Other Foreign Air Forces (AS/AS- Series)

description: Notes by A[rthur] Cadbury-Jones about a visit to his office at 22-24 Glasshouse Street, Piccadilly, London W from [Aleister] Crowley three years before. Crowley mentioned using Dr William Wynn Westcott's name in a book he intended publishing but Cadbury-Jones referred to several letters in which he had informed Crowley that Westcott would not permit Crowley to cite. Crowley mentioned the Cipher MSS, which he wanted to place on deposit at the British Museum. Although the property of Westcott, Crowley wished to make the Cipher MSS accessible to others in order to share their secrets and to confirm if they were forgeries or genuine. Crowley made reference to the Horos Case. Cadbury-Jones had warned Crowley about accusations of slander and libel which might cause him problems and Crowley mentioned a visit from the police who had seized some of his books which were later returned. Cadbury-Jones informed Crowley that Westcott had resigned from the Golden Dawn and had not had access to the papers of the Society for some time. Crowley asked Cadbury-Jones if Westcott was under oath to [Samuel Liddell MacGregor] Mathers not to divulge the Cipher MSS and that Westcott had shown him a document of allegiance to Mathers but Cadbury-Jones did not know anything about that. Crowley spoke against Westcott but Cadbury-Jones informed Crowley that he was making a mountain out of a mole hill through his own imagination. Cadbury-Jones informed Crowley that his previous work had already mentioned and damaged Westcott and he should cease his actions. Crowley informed Casbury-Jones that certificates were being issued with [Samuel Liddell MaGregor] Mathers as Chief and Westcott as Second which might constitute a fraud. Crowley was advised not to write or publish anything including Westcott's name and Crowley left after thirty minutes.
title: Notes by Arthur Cadbury Jones about visit of Crowley to his office

description: Photographs of an envelope and note sent anonymously to Dr W. Wynn Westcott. The envelope is stamped with a postmark from Liège, Belgium, dated 3 August 1900. [‘S Rioghail Mo Dhream, 5=6 motto of S. L. Mathers] has forfeit the help of the Chiefs of R. R. et A.C. Ellic Howe suggests in his book Magicians of the Golden Dawn ‘that as the handwriting appears to be that of an educated Englishman rather than a Belgian, Westcott must have been a victim of a practical joke’. description: At the time the correspondence begins in 1944 Joseph Stephens was 19 years old, and was based in Yorkshire where he was completing his training as a Cipher Clerk in the Royal Signals Regiment. He was born in January 1926, and educated at Kingswood School, near Bath, a school founded by John Wesley for the sons of Methodist Ministers. His family was devoutly Methodist and Joseph contemplated entering the Ministry after demobilisation. His parents owned a shop in Downend, Bristol and he had two younger brothers (Philip and John) and a sister (Rachel). He departed for India in October 1945 and after a brief quarantine in Bombay travelled in early December to Mhow in Madhya Pradesh, for initial training. At the end of December he was transferred to Rawalpindi in the Punjab. He remained there until May 1946, when he was transferred to Kohat, capital of the Kohat District in the Khyber province of what is now Pakistan. In July 1946 he was posted to Abbottabad to open up a new cipher office. Abbottabad is in the Hazara region of eastern Khyber, about 120 kilometres north of Rawalpindi. In September 1946 he takes a month's leave in Kashmir. He remained in Abbottabad until May 1947 when he was transferred to Peshawar, near the Khyber Pass. This is shortly before Independence (August 1947) and he was required to train Indian personnel as cipher operators. By November he was in Karachi transit camp and left India to return to Britain in December 1947. This collection consists of photographs taken by or on behalf of Stephens during his time in Northern India, which generally show scenes around him, the natural environment, the men he was serving with etc. It also contains over 200 letters written by Stephens to his family, and other papers mainly relating to his time in India.
title: Stephens collection

description: "I do not well know how long the business will hold me at Athlone, but from thence your Lordship shall hear from me with all expedition; nor I do not know whether I shall be well able to meet you as far as Lymrick, the which I will if possible I can, but you must prepare yourself to meet me either there or at Gallaway, for I must needs speak with you. And because it is meet that you should think of it before-hand, and determine of all things accordingly, I think I must send you immediately from thence into England. I had rather carry you back with me to Dublin and to despatch you from thence, but it shall be at your choice; but, if it be possible, prepare to go from Dublin. I know this will be no evil news unto you, and therefore I make the more haste to send it. Let me hear from you presently. Your letters, God willing shall find me at Athlone or Galloway." Trim, 6 December 1602. Addressed. Endorsed. The words in Italics are in cipher, deciphered by Carew. [The cipher used in these letters is very simple. The letter g is used for a, h for b, and so on, i and j being treated as one letter, as also u and v.]
title: LORD DEPUTY MOUNTJOY to SIR GEORGE CAREW.

description: By the arrival of your servant Harvie, I had some intelligence of your being upon this coast; by whom I sent a letter, which I hope is come to your hands. Having this day received yours dated at Kinsall the 7th, with another from the Privy Council, I now stand assured of your being there. The Dingle and the mouth of the Shenen are the aptest places for those ships to remain in; for as at the Dingle the landing of foreign aid is expected, so is the Shenen the only mean either for our meeting, or safe convoying of our letters. If with safety you may not come to this town (from whence my weakness will not yet suffer me to depart), send with all speed a copy of your instructions. As for my knowledge of foreign advertisements, I have written such as I learned to her Majesty and the Lords; "and such as is brought me by one who was in Spain with Sidere [Captain James Sidee. See also 21 April.] I suppose is neither hid from their Lls., nor yourself are ignorant of." Mr. Treasurer, by his own letter, has fully delivered his mind for the money by you brought. I have made very hard shift to victual this bearer, Captain Yorke. Limerick, 15 April 1580. Signed. Postscript.--Because you may the better write in covert, I send you a cipher herewith closed. Here follows the cipher referred to. Contemp. copy.
title: PELHAM to SIR WILLIAM WINTER.

description: This deposit comprises two series of diaries - of Lieut.-Gen. Sir F.W.N. McCracken and of his wife Ann ('Nan'), daughter of T.C. Glover of Edinburgh - together with a small number of other documents and papers. General McCracken's diaries cover the period 1882-1938, with a short gap for the duration of the first World War, 1914-1918. They provide a detailed record both of his family life and of his military career during this time. They are, however, essentially personal documents: comparatively little note is taken of public events. There are many loose papers and other items in the diaries - telegrams, letters, visiting cards and programmes, as well as rough notes and jottings. These have not generally been noted in detail except in the case of letters and photographs. Occasionally pressed flowers have been found between the pages of the diary: these have generally been removed for better preservation. Mrs. McCracken's diaries cover the period 1886-1912, though the series is very incomplete after 1897. A considerable part of these diaries has been written in a cypher. This has been deciphered by Miss F.S. Stradling, M.A., who has also provided the following note on the diaries: Ciphers such as this are common in diaries and writings of the late nineteenth century and were particularly popular among women. It is not known where this cipher originated - possibly it was devised by Mrs. McCracken herself. It is in any case quite a straightforward cipher: some letters remain the same, others are upside down, and others are replaced by symbols. The same cipher can also be found in certain entries of General McCracken's diaries, especially during the period between his engagement and marriage. Mrs. McCracken's diaries begin in January 1886. For the first two years, 1886 and 1887, they are particularly detailed, covering the period of her courtship and early marriage. As the duties of marriage and motherhood become more pressing the entries become briefer and some of the lively detail of the earlier entries is lost. At the beginning of 1886 the Glover family are in Hoshungabad, India. There is no means of telling, from the diaries themselves, in what capacity Mr. Glover is there, but frequent references to 'accompanying Papa to the workshop' suggest perhaps that it is in a commercial rather than a military capacity. Life for Ann Glover consists largely of helping Mama, playing tennis, and attending (and giving) numerous dinners and dances. Her social life is very full and she is very susceptible to the attentions of young men. There are many references to army personnel, and the family's social life obviously is centred in army circles. Anyone with the patience to decipher Nan McCracken's diaries will find their efforts rewarded. Although the style is rather pedestrian and they are not perhaps of the highest literary quality, nevertheless they are full of detail and create a surprisingly real picture of colonial life. Besides the two main series of diaries there is a short series of pocket diaries, 1927-1932, and two volumes containing a private log of sea voyages round South America, 1926 and undated, both kept by General McCracken, two volumes containing notes on 'Health Lectures', and on astronomy, geology and botany, kept by Mrs. McCracken, and a small number of miscellaneous Christmas cards, visiting cards and other papers.
title: Diaries and other papers of Lt. Gen. Sir Frederick McCracken (1859-1949) and of Mrs. Ann ('Nan') McCracken (d. 1923)

description: Sent by Hoper of Barstable. I have sent your Highness a cipher herein closed, because it may be doubted how letters will come to my hands, when I shall be encamped far from the port-towns. The causes are these. First, forasmuch as I have discovered many arguments that the rebels are weary of the war, and are doubtful of the forces coming against them, insomuch as the Earl and his brethren come not together but upon oath and a kind of protection, and have their followers apart, mistrusting also Saunders to have come with false persuasion from foreign princes,--I desire to be directed from your Majesty that if the Earl of Desmond shall secretly offer any such humble submission as may carry with it honour to your Majesty, with the delivery of his brothers, Sanders, and other of the principal rebels, whereby quietness may follow, whether with any such terms I may receive him to your Majesty's mercy. Secondly, whereas it is certain that some of the Lords, pretending to do your Majesty service, and yet as far in the confederacy as those in open action, do suffer the rebels to live in their countries, [and to] feed upon their tenants in so small numbers as they might withstand and overthrow at their pleasures,--whether I may not apprehend such, and either send them into England, there to know the greatness of their sovereign, or to Dublin, there to be tried upon their misbehaviours, and what manner of trial I shall allow to such; of which sort, to make it plain to your Majesty, the Earl of Clancare and the Lo. Barrie will be (as I am informed) manifestly detected. Thirdly, whether the noblemen's sons in Munster, being now pledges in Cork and other places, and such other as I think good shortly to possess myself of for the assurance of their inconstant fathers, may not be sent prisoners into England to some place of strength, to work the more effectual dealings in their parents, who find such friendship in all cities of this realm, as they make no accompt of the restraint of their children in those places either for terror or any hard dealing. Farther, whether if the Countess of Desmond sue to go over to your Majesty as she hath of late pretended, having as I hear furnished herself with the plate of Youghall to bear her charges either in Spain or England, whether I may license her so to do or not, for the ports are so laid, as she will hardly adventure to do it without license. Lastly, I desire to know your Majesty's resolution, what course of government shall be taken in this province of Munster, and who shall be left governor amongst them, when God shall give an end of these wars, which either in one kind or other I hope shall be in short time after the supply of all our wants. Waterford, the last of January 1579. Signed. II. "A Cipher sent to her Majesty." [13 of the ciphers "signify nothing;" 18 are equivalent to certain common words of one syllable; and 43 represent the names of so many important persons and places. There are, moreover, two ciphers for each letter of the alphabet.] Contemp. copy.
title: PELHAM to the QUEEN.

Discusses measures for settling the payment for the Canada paper money in Europe and encloses copies of the two decrees of the Conseil d'Etat [ff.31, 33] referred to in f.17. Praslin believed France had complied with everything requested in SP 78/268, ff.275, 277 but was unwilling to give a written agreement and Richmond would not assume agreement without one. Praslin said that the parents of the children detained as converts must have recourse to law in order to establish reciprocity with English practice. Choiseul denies Britain's right to destroy the jetties and the remains of the forts at Dunkirk, basing his argument on his interpretation of treaties. Encloses letters for the king. Friesland agrees to war measures. Frenchmen apply for letters of marque from the Dutch, but some from Dunkirk have obtained the same from the English. English naval preparations. description: Folio 97v. Stepney to Blathwayt. Largely similar to f.92v, but adding certain details of his conversation with Kinsky when the latter handed him the [intercepted] letter from Chateauneuf to the French king (see f.90v). The particulars Kinsky communicated to him served the purpose to warn both Heemskerck and Paget about bringing Thököly, his person and estate into any peace proposals or treaty. He, Stepney, thinks it most unlikely that Heemskerck would have reacted favourably to any overtures by Thököly, he would have acted in direct contradiction to the proposals he exhibited to the grand vizier on Oct 13 at Belgrade. The fifth article of the document expressly demands that 'Teckelius caput rebellium, qui hujus belli ansam praebuit, inter spatium duarum mensium post pacem conclusam tradatur'. As regards Paget, he had even 'less temptations to befriend Teckely' against whom he has personal grudges. Kinsky requested him to press Paget to enquire what more considerable pension, presents or subsidies he [i.e. Thököly] might receive from France 'for that summe [10,000 crowns] as but a very pitifull reward for the services he does them'. Count [Gottlieb] Windischgraetz is to be grand-master of the imperial household and is to be replaced by count [Dominic Andrew] Kaunitz as envoy at the Hague. Count [Leopold] Auersperg is to be envoy to London, he is to meet the King in the Netherlands. Requests, in cipher, instructions, also in cipher, if the king should be 'inclined to shew any sort of favour to count Teckely'. But if he, Stepney, is specially to instruct Heemskerck not to concern himself in Thököly's behalf, the instructions asked for should be 'at large' so that he can show them to Kinsky. Date and Place: 1693 July 22/Aug 1 Vienna.

description: Nathalie SERGUEIEW, alias Lily, codename TREASURE; French. SERGUEIEW, a pre-war journalist based in Paris, offered her services to an acquaintance working for German Intelligence with the express intention of double-crossing them. After lengthy training by the Abwehr she travelled to Spain where she made contact with British Intelligence and came to England in 1943. Here she became an important Double Cross agent for MI5 and was used as a channel for deception. Material passed over her radio included reports designed to mislead the enemy regarding troop assembly in Southern England prior to D-Day. Her radio link to her German controller in Paris was used by MI5 right up to the liberation of that city.

description: Folio 22: Whitworth to Stanhope. Secret. Whitworth explains to King of Prussia in an audience with him the overtures which Heusch is to make, to renew the alliance with George as Elector of Brunswick and, as guarantor, as King of England. King refers decision to ministers, who eventually approve, with reservations, except for one article regarding peace to be made with certain Northern powers in which they wished to include the Czar. Unwillingness to name King of Poland in the article. Rothembourg reveals Prussian intention to send Schwerin as minister to the court of Sweden, considers that Schwerin is a person inimical to the king. Ilgen tells Schwerin the plan depends on outcome of negotiations with Whitworth. Heusch and Whitworth feel that the plan for Peace in the North should be suppressed. From Berlin.

Bollavin pursues his policy of ruling as a deputy of the Czar. Baskir Tartars have been appeased by the concessions of the government. context: STANDISH PAPERS.
description: Lancashire was particularly strong in its Jacobite sympathies, and one of the leading plots to restore James II to the English throne was centred around Standish Hall. The following papers - mainly correspondence and blank commissions relating to the projected Jacobite invasions - were found in a garden wall at Standish Hall in 1757, where they had been hidden some 60 years earlier. Had they been available to the Crown then, it is most unlikely that the conspirators would have been acquitted at their trial in Manchester in 1694. Even after they had been discovered, some of the papers could not be read for over a century and a half, as they were in cipher, the key to which was only discovered in 1927, by Rev. T.C. Porteus. See his 'New Light on the Lancashire Jacobite Plot, 1692-4', in Transactions of the Lancashire and Cheshire Antiquarian Society, vol. L. (available in the Record Office library) for further background information, and transcriptions of the correspondence
title: STANDISH PLOT PAPERS

context: THE BRAY FAMILY OF SHERE: ESTATE AND FAMILY RECORDS AND COLLECTED PAPERS INCLUDING OF THE...PAPERS OF THE NICHOLAS FAMILY OF WEST HORSLEY.
description: John Nicholas (b. 1624) was educated at Queen's College, Oxford, and was then (1644) sent to France, where his father joined him in 1646. He worked as secretary to Edward Hyde (1653-58), and is said to have helped him in writing his history. Early in 1655 he was ordered to keep the King's ciphers (D Nicholas, Mr Secretary Nicholas (1955) p.274). He returned to England in 1660 in the royal party and was made a Knight of the Bath in the Restoration honours, becoming one of the Clerks to the Privy Council, and MP for Wilton in 1661. He married Lady Penelope Compton, and died in 1704. Many of his papers are in the Nicholas collection (Egerton MSS 2533-2562) in the British Library, and others are in the John Rylands Library, Manchester (ref R 45817/75-6 & 86). His London house was in Spring Gardens, Westminster. Letters are endorsed with name of correspondent, and date
title: LETTERS TO SIR JOHN NICHOLAS

context: Manuscripts.Carew Manuscripts.Carew Manuscript.
description: Sent by Ferreie, the Pursuivant. I have received your letters by Ferraie, your pursuivant, together with your direction in Mr. Secretary's letter in cipher. The traitor Sir James of Desmond is mortally wounded and taken prisoner, and the most part of his forces slain and overthrown, the 4th of this month, by Sir Cormoke McTeige, sheriff of your county of Cork. Some other encounters have been since the arrival of your pursuivant, wherein the rebels have sustained loss by your garrison of Kilmalloke; in one of which Doctor Sanders and John of Desmond did make a strange escape, being in the night above an hour in their company preserved in the dark by speaking English, and crying upon the English to execute the Irish. Sanders' man (born in Chester) and an Irish friar, standard bearer (as he was termed) unto James FitzMorris, were apprehended, whereof the first slain by the fury of the soldiers, and the other reserved to farther examination. Touching my manner of prosecuting, it is thus: I give the rebels no breath to relieve themselves, but by one of your garrisons or other they be continually hunted. I keep them from their harvest, and have taken great preys of cattle from them, by which it seemeth the poor people that lived only upon labour, and fed by their milch cows, are so distressed, as they follow their goods and offer themselves with their wives and children rather to be slain by the army than to suffer the famine that now in extremity beginneth to pinch them. And the calamity of these things have made a division between the Earl and John of Desmond, John and Sanders seeking for relief to fall into the company and fellowship of the Viscount Baltinglas; and the Earl, without rest anywhere, flieth from place to place, and maketh mediation for peace by the Countess, who yesterday I licensed to have speech with me here, whose abundance of tears betrayed sufficiently the miserable estate both of herself, her husband, and their followers, whereof I write more in cipher to Mr. Secretary. Asketten, 12 August 1580. Signed. Contemp. copy.
title: LORD JUSTICE PELHAM to the QUEEN.

context: Records of the Communications Department.
adminHistory: Until 1824 the Foreign Office had no messengers for its own exclusive use, but shared them with the Home and Colonial Offices. In 1824 the messengers were divided into Home Service and Foreign Service messengers, some of the former and all of the latter being assigned to the Foreign Office, where the librarian was made superintendent of king's messengers. In 1854 the superintendence was transferred to the chief clerk. In 1919 a separate King's Messengers and Communications Department was set up to be responsible for the messengers, mails and for ciphering and deciphering (which had been undertaken in the Parliamentary Department since 1911); in 1922 this became the Communications Department. In 1965, with the formation of the Diplomatic Service, the Communications Department was transferred to the newly formed Diplomatic Service Administration Office where it was amalgamated with the Commonwealth Relations Office Communications Department and dealt with communications matters for the Foreign Office, the Commonwealth Relations Office and the British Trade Commissions.
description: Records of the Foreign Office and Diplomatic Service Administration Office Communications Department after 1936 are in FO 850.
title: Records of the Communications Department

context: Prime Minister's Office: Sir Desmond Morton, Personal Assistant to Prime Minister: Correspondence and Minutes.
adminHistory: Major Sir Desmond John Falkiner Morton (1891-1971) entered the Foreign Office as an intelligence officer in 1919 following a distinguished military service during which time he came to the notice of Winston Churchill. He formed a personal friendship with Churchill, assisting him with The World Crisis (5 vols, 1923-1931). Throughout the 1930s, he was Churchill's close adviser, In 1932, he obtained the permission of the Prime Minister (Ramsay MacDonald) to provide Churchill with certain confidential reports and information. This arrangement was subsequently endorsed and continued by the two succeeding Prime Ministers (Baldwin and Chamberlain), and was of considerable value to Churchill's campaign for British rearmament. In May 1940, on becoming Prime Minister, Churchill made Morton his personal assistant, a role which Morton continued throughout the Second World War. During this period, he filtered information to Churchill received from breaching of the German 'Enigma' cipher.

From the detaining of these lords many good effects have ensued. The wars of Munster are reduced to a declining state; the traitors suffering privation of many succours which they before enjoyed. description: Folio 148: De Bacquoy to [Bennet]. Dutch have no lack of sailors. They are continuing to keep their merchant vessels in port. Those in foreign ports will be escorted home in convoys. War material from Sweden has not yet arrived in England due to ice preventing passage of shipping, and Dutch hope to intercept them. Louis XIV insists that a Dutch vessel taken by the English close off Boulogne should be returned. Dutch have told the Hanse towns that in their opinion the English have no right to try and interfere with their trade. Banckert's expedition resulted in two ships being wrecked, while crews in the others suffered from the harsh weather and [plague]. The Governor of Maestricht, Ryngrave, is at the Hague trying to prove himself innocent of having planned to give the city to the French, as Richart, the Spanish Royal Secretary for the Spanish Netherlands alleges. description: Folio 39: Downing to Bennet. Warns that De Ruyter may attack English possessions and shipping in the West Indies or North America. Believes England is in a better position to fight a sustained war, as the United Provinces are heavily populated with limited land, and so more dependant on trade, while Dutch ships, unlike those of England, have to run the gauntlet of an English blockade. Much of the money in the United Provinces is owned by foreigners who can be expected to leave if the war is protracted. Dutch taxes already very high. Believes Holland will be left to bear the brunt of financing the war, as Zeeland is too poor to contribute much, while the other Provinces are unwilling to do so. Dutch believe England can ruin them by blockade alone. Dutch plan to send more warships to the Mediterranean. English seizure of French wine might antagonise France, yet returning it might encourage the Dutch to carry on their trade in foreign ships. Advises giving reassurances to Dutch residents in England, and allowing them to become naturalized. Dutch hopes of French mediation. Dutch East India Company hopes to ruin English trade in the East Indies. Dutch propaganda about maltreatment of imprisoned Dutch sailors in England; he suggests `the truth' should be better presented. Date and place: Jan 24/Feb 4 Hague.

description: The 12th I received your letters, and the 13th despatched Pavie again with answer. I was afraid the store in Cork was not so strong as it is, and am exceeding glad the proportion of powder you sent for is not defective in anything. "The state of the victuals I have commanded to be sent unto your Lordship, whereof your Lordship may dispose at your pleasure. I would have sent Jollye, the master gunner, unto your Lordship, but all the ordnance and munition was delivered into his charge, and I had no conveniency to rummage it, not having any cover for it, being brought ashore (as of necessity it must be if his charge had been committed to another man), but the open firmament. Besides, being so near Donboye, where his service was of use, I was bold to detain him until the service were ended, meaning then to send him to your Lordship with all possible expedition, which, by God's grace, shall be precisely performed. But since that time it hath so pleased God to lay his cross upon us, as I have lost the best cannonier in my opinion that England these many years hath bred; his name was Parker, and sent unto your Lordship, by my assignment, purposely hither, who this day died; whereby I have none but Jollye left to effect the service pretended. When Pavye was here Parker was sick. If Jolly could by any means have delivered over his charge for the which he indented, no occasion should have moved me to have stayed him. "My hope was, the day after Pavye's departure, to have crossed with the forces the Bay of Bantry; by which means I should have escaped all the straits and places of advantage possessed by the enemy. But it pleased God otherwise to determine, for since the 15th.. to this present we have had the extremest weather that I have seen, nothing differing from the depth of winter but the shortness of the night. In the memory of man I do not think such a continual storm of wind and rain in May hath been seen seen, perpetually at the south-west, so as neither ship nor boat could move from their anchors without imminent peril of loss, and if the harbour were not excellent good, I think some of them would have perished as they rode. "If Archer have the art of conjuring I think he hath not been idle, but, ere it be long, I hope to conjure him, for I am informed that he protests to abide the siege in the castle. By some of the Irish that came out of the eastle of Donboye unto me I am informed that they have ramparted the castle round about within their barbican eighteen foot in thickness as high as the top of the barbican, and thereupon have raised a parapet of earth; upon this rampart they have placed their artillery, and have taken down the castle to the vault, which is a pike length above the rampart of their barbican. This work will give us impediment in the planting of our battery, but I hope, when the ordnance is planted, it will prove their confusion, for the remainder of the height of the castle will, by the ruins of it, quickly take away the use of their ordnance, and the castle cannot annoy us, for the rampart unto the height of the barbican hath taken from them the use of all their spikes and lower fightes, so as they will live but in a dungeon, out of the which, with the pickaxe, we shall conveniently remove them. To give us further labour, they do now fortify in the island of the Dursies, seven miles to the westward of Donboye, unto the which place they have carried three pieces of ordnance. But of the one and the other I hope to give your Lordship a good account. "All Kerry and Desmond is reduced, and since the death of Dermod Moyle McCartie, Florence his brother, who was slain the 13th of this present, the Munster men are out of heart, and sue to be received to mercy; which unto landed men I do refuse, for the rest upon assurance I receive. Of the ancient rebels there is McMorrice, John FitzThomas, and the Knight of the Valley; of the late revolters, O'Solevan Beare, the Knight of Kerry, Thomas Oge FitzGerald, O'Connor Kerry, and Sir Fynnyn O'Driscoll's eldest son. But they are all exceeding poor, and among them not above 400 provincials. "With Terrell and William Bourke there is of buonies 1,200 by poll, who live only upon O'Solevan's creaghts, which by our lodging so near them is almost consumed and cannot long continue. All the subjects' cattle from Kynsale westward I have caused to be removed into the east part of the county of Corke. So all Carbry, Desmond, and Dowalla, and most part of Muskerry, is left waste, whereby the buonyes of force must after a little while depart from hence. They are exceeding weary, and would fain be gone, but Archer every day devises letters and intelligences out of Spain, assuring them of succours, and once a week confirms new leagues, and seals them with the sacrament. Yet nevertheless divers of their men come daily unto me and run from them. "When Donboye is once taken, I am sure they will leave this province and seek some other fortune, which they are unwilling to do, not knowing where else in Ireland to get any bonnaght. Tyrrell, to have a company in pay, would come from them; which, without service to deserve so great a favour, I deny, and service he will do none, thinking that he merits sufficiently by leaving them. William Burke stands upon the same terms, and therefore they must run one fortune. "If your Lordship be remembered, one James Blake [In cipher.] of Galwaye [In cipher.] desired your Lordship's protection to come unto to you to Corke, but before his coming thither your Lordship was gone. Afterwards he required the like from me, and he came unto me. After much speech, protesting innocency and integrity, to clear himself of all suspicion, he took a solemn oath to do service that should merit good opinion and reward. Having no cause known unto me of any fact by him committed, nor yet having power to detain him, because he came unto me upon.. protection, I applauded his enterprise, whereupon he departed from me, and is gone into Spain, [In cipher.] with a determination (bound with many oaths) to kill O'Donnell. [In cipher.] That he is gone I am sure by those that were embarked [In cipher.] with him. God give him strength and perseverance. If a man may judge of resolution by external appearance and protestations, he will effect his business; if not, there is nothing lost. I told him that I would acquaint your Lordship with it, and that but unto your Lordship I would not acquaint any man with his purpose. "I understand that long since your Lordship sent a pursuivant unto me with letters, and in them letters which came from Don Juan del Aquila to your Lordship, but I have not received them. I am informed that he departed Corke, but I fear he is slain upon the way, for of such letters sent unto me I have had report out of the rebels' camp. If your Lordship write again.. direct that from Corke or Kynsale they may be sent by sea. And yet, since Florence's brother was slain, six men may pass from Kynsale to Bantry, but no further." Again "I pray your Lordship to continue Cormocke and John Barry in pay until the siege at Donboye be ended. I dare not let them know your pleasure, foreseeing the mischief that will ensue before that service be ended. The parties to me are the children of Adam, and one of them your Lordship knows my opinion of him." P.S.--"The private business committed by your Lordship unto Pavie is despatched, and he having with him four hundred in Spanish money, [In cipher.] your Lordship in my opinion for a little while (until the rumour of the coming of Spaniards is forgotten or not to be feared) [would do well] to continue a running post between Corke and Dublin. The charge will not be great, considering the shortness of the time." "At the camp near the Abbey of Bantry, 28 May 1602." Copy.
title: SIR GEORGE CAREW to LORD DEPUTY MOUNTJOY.

description: Folio 27. Stepney to Sir William [Dutton] Colt [at Dresden]. Refers to a count de Monceau, being, apparently in some kind of detention at Prague and for whom he declines to intercede: '. the true spring of his disgrace is his being too zealous a servant to Feld Marshall Schöning'. Speculates, at some length, on the efforts to obtain the assistance of the elector of Saxony, who 'bargains hard', in the war against France, his inferences largely based on information given him by Baron [Otto-Heinrich von] Friesen [the elector's envoy designate to the States General, passing through Vienna]. Before the elector will decide anything, he will want to know 1) where the troops are to act, 2) with whom they are to join, 3) how they will be commanded, 4) what subsidies they will receive, and 5) whether they will have their winter quarters on the Rhine or return home after the summer campaign. Comments on these points in a pessimistic vein, pointing out, inter alia, that the Saxon forces would be most active only on the Middle Rhine between Heidelberg and Coblentz and be joined mainly by the Hanoverians, and foresees impediments to progress such as: the liberty of Schöning against whom there are only strong suspicions and as yet no real proofs; abandonment of the duke of Saxony-Merseburg [Christian II], the elector no longer trying to 'espouse the interest of the several small branches to the prejudice of the electoral family; the elector's tendency to resolve the dispute over Saxony-Lauenburg; and the elevation of Miss Neidschütz, the elector's mistress, 'supposed to be with child', to the dignity of countess of the Empire, that dignity to be continued to her posterity. Urges Colt to strictest secrecy and warns him not to report about these matters to Whitehall and to use cipher in mentioning them in reply to himself. Observes that if the elector's wish is not granted, it may 'spoil all, so fully is that Elector of King Charles' his humour who sacrificed the interest of state to his pleasures and vices', and advises Colt to make his 'court to that lady [Miss Neidschütz]. Speculates further on the Emperor's possible reaction to the elector's pretences. Has seen a letter from [Albrecht Philipp von dem] Bussche [Hanoverian minister and privy councillor, which makes him apprehend 'as if the D[uke] of Wolfenbuttle had received French money and has no longer his hands free and I must confess Mr [Rudolph Christian, baron von] Imhoff, his minister here, acts as if this were true by entering into the Cabal of the ministers of Denmark, and Münster and being as violent as either of them' [Relevant para marked as having originally been in cipher]. Date and Place: 1693 Jan 25 Vienna.

description: Folio 131: De Bacquoy to [Bennet]. He is angered by the delay to the delivery of his last dispatches and suggests better arrangements. Believes that if the war lasts three years England could dictate terms to the Dutch, because of their financial predicament and widespread unemployment. Dutch diplomatic dispatches from England sent by circuitous route to avoid interception. Cuneus made soundings amongst influential Englishmen, but found little disposition for compromise or peace, so the States General have ordered him to cease this activity until a more propitious time. Duke of York and Prince Rupert will personally command the English fleet and Killigrew's regiment of 4,000 men will be ready to embark aboard the warships. England has not found enough privateers as yet. Pressing continues. Four thousand musqueteers in addition to the marines will impose a logistical burden in supplying sufficient provisions to the English fleet. Dutch have asked Spain and Tuscany for port facilities and access to provisions for their warships. English ships observed off Nieuport and Ostend. Zeeland is insisting that the banner of their Lieutenant Admiral Jan Everts should not be put behind those of Holland's new Lieutenant Admirals. Further Dutch recruitment to strengthen frontiers, and finance for action against Barbary pirates. Augmentation of infantry companies and recruitment of German and Swiss mercenaries. De Bacquoy asks that he be paid for his expenses. Date and place: 1665 Feb 18 [OS or NS] [Leeuwarden].

description: ALAN TURING WARTIME RESEARCH PAPERS RELEASED BY GCHQ'The Applications of Probability to Crypt'As the country marks the centenary of Alan Turing's birth, two of his mathematical research papers, believed to have been written whilst he was at Bletchley Park during World War II, have been released by GCHQ to The National Archives.Because of continuing sensitivity the papers had been retained at GCHQ, but they have now been reassessed as suitable for release. The papers, called 'Paper on Statistics of Repetitions' and 'The Applications of Probability to Crypt', were written in an era when typographical errors would be corrected by hand and mathematical notation handwritten.The first, 'Paper on Statistics of Repetitions', is an informal report in which Turing works out the best statistical means of testing whether two cipher messages use the same key in parts of the message. This was very important in the exploitation of such messages at Bletchley Park.The second, longer, paper titled 'The Applications of Probability to Cryptography', demonstrates that Turing was determined to apply rigorous probability analysis to a wide range of cryptanalytic problems of the day. A particular highlight is where Turing uses life expectancy to examine conditional probability. The associated example, 'Hitler is now of age 52', adds piquancy and suggests that the paper was written between April 1941 and April 1942. Bletchley Park's output of decrypts was almost certainly enabled by the techniques in this paper.

adminHistory: Sir Frank Ezra Adcock (1886-1968) was a historian of Greece and Rome. He was born at Desford, Leicestershire, the son of Thomas Draper Adcock, schoolmaster, head of the Desford Industrial School, and his wife, Mary Esther Coltman. He was educated at Wyggeston grammar school, Leicester, and King’s College Cambridge. In 1911, he was elected a fellow of his college and appointed a lecturer in classics in 1911. During World War I he worked for the intelligence division of the Admiralty as an interpreter of codes and ciphers. After the war, he became an editor of Cambridge Ancient History journal and was its chief editor from 1927 until his death. In 1925 he became the chair of Ancient History at Cambridge. During World War II, he was release from his chair to work for the Foreign Office. He returned to Cambridge in 1943 and became the president of the Classical Association from 1951-1955. He retired in 1951 and was knighted in 1954. Although he frequently contributed to Cambridge Ancient History, he rarely published his research elsewhere. He died in Cambridge on 22 February 1968.

description: Collection of pamphlets and offprints collected by Sir Frank Ezra Adcock (1886- 1968) mostly relating to the history of Ancient Greece and Rome. Includes offprints sent to by Adcock by their authors. The collection has been arranged alphabetically by author. Also includes some corespondence and notes by Adcock.

description: Folio 9: De Bacquoy to [Bennet]. Dutchmen who wish to see the fall of De Witt and restoration of the Prince of Orange are delighted at indications that France will not honour its treaty obligation to the United Provinces, excusing itself by claiming that the Dutch expedition to West Africa provoked English aggression in the Channel. De Witt seems to be trying to encourage and arm Anabaptists and other frenetiques to rise up against Charles II. Hopes De Witt will be blamed for causing the war and for opposing the restitution of the Prince of Orange to the position he formerly held. Dutch Council of State recommends that a greater number of warships be made ready than recommended previously. It is proposed to send three deputies from the States General and a deputy from each of the Admiralties aboard the Dutch fleet to ensure better discipline and determination. France may support Dutch. Dutch will cashier English and Scottish soldiers in their pay. Zeeland wants letters of marque to be issued; fears that if this is delayed, potential privateers assembled at Ostend may join the English side. English have apparently already issued letters of marque. De Ruyter' success on West African coast; he is expected to head for home soon. France prevaricates in reply to Dutch request for assistance. description: ALAN TURING WARTIME RESEARCH PAPERS RELEASED BY GCHQ'Paper on Statistics of Repetitions' As the country marks the centenary of Alan Turing's birth, two of his mathematical research papers, believed to have been written whilst he was at Bletchley Park during World War II, have been released by GCHQ to The National Archives.Because of continuing sensitivity the papers had been retained at GCHQ, but they have now been reassessed as suitable for release. The papers, called 'Paper on Statistics of Repetitions' and 'The Applications of Probability to Crypt', were written in an era when typographical errors would be corrected by hand and mathematical notation handwritten.The first, 'Paper on Statistics of Repetitions', is an informal report in which Turing works out the best statistical means of testing whether two cipher messages use the same key in parts of the message. This was very important in the exploitation of such messages at Bletchley Park.The second, longer, paper titled 'The Applications of Probability to Cryptography', demonstrates that Turing was determined to apply rigorous probability analysis to a wide range of cryptanalytic problems of the day. A particular highlight is where Turing uses life expectancy to examine conditional probability. The associated example, 'Hitler is now of age 52', adds piquancy and suggests that the paper was written between April 1941 and April 1942. Bletchley Park's output of decrypts was almost certainly enabled by the techniques in this paper.

description: Folio 112: Downing to Bennet. Plague spreads in the United Provinces including `the best houses', 905 deaths in Amsterdam alone. Dutch have lost hopes of gaining the alliance of Sweden and Denmark and are consequently unlikely to yield concessions to them. States accept Louis XIV's offer to mediate. Holland supplies ships to assist the Dutch West Indies Company. Dutch protest over Cape Verde presented to Downing. De Witt stifled debate over Cayana (Cayenne) since the Dutch do not wish to offend France. Dutch fear English may take over the West African gold and slave trade completely. Thinks Scotland's decision to prohibit all trade with the United Provinces for fear of contracting the plague is a wise one. Downing evades De Witt's request for a reply over Cape Verde and an official paper to protect the Dutch against the English fleet sailing to West Africa, suggesting that only an overall settlement will stop further hostilities there. Downing thinks an agreement would be advantageous to the Royal Africa Company but hopes that during the negotiations `Holmes will doe the work there', and does not believe the Dutch will hold to any agreement. `Never will be such a opportunity as this to make clear work in Africa.' Recalls earlier Dutch claim to the whole coast and trade of West Africa by Valkenburg. Date and place: 1660 Aug 4/14 Hague.

description: Sent by Mr. Maie. Ormond has sent me letters received from the Lord Roche. The news of the Spanish practice is confirmed. "The Earl came in person to his house in Kerrie, called the Island, to have conference with those messengers that were sent unto him, both French and Spanish." Every man in Munster is persuaded of foreign aid. Many gentlemen and freeholders of the county of Limerick are fled to the rebels. A general revolt is to be feared as soon as any foreign aid shall come. The towns are for the more part weak. Should the town of Dingle be fortified to withstand the landing of the Spaniards ? As our soldiers are dispersed into many places, a strong fleet should be kept upon the seas to keep those channels free. Food is growing scarce in Munster. Instead of cattle and garrons, I am compelled to levy 300 churles, upon whose backs I carry all my provision to the field. I hear that some treasure is arrived at Dublin. When I shall pass from this port towards Limerick, I shall hardly send letters but with hazard; the only sure way will be by water up the Shenen to Athlone, and so to Dublin. It may be doubted how the Pale itself will be affected, if they stand assured of foreign invasion. I have sent a cipher enclosed. Waterford, 11 February 1579. Signed. Contemp. copy.
title: PELHAM to the COUNCIL in ENGLAND.

adminHistory: Arthur Bolton (1868-1910) son of Jasper Bolton and Emily (nee Grey) youngest sister of Josephine Butler. He entered the Royal Navy as an engineer officer. Constance was his sister and she married Dr Frank Hudson Biog: Amelie Humbert , Swinburne, James Stuart, Frank and Constance Hudson
description: Photocopy of letter. Written from Hotel Bellevue, Neuchatel The hotel is deserted and she feels very lonely, though Miss Humbert comes daily to see her. There is deep snow and everyone gets about in sleighs which make no noise except for 'the elegant jingling turn out' of the 'young Suchard gentleman (chocolate).' Recalls how one day at Wimbledon when she and Rhoda were out together, they met Swinburne, the Poet, walking along, and Rhoda was so disgusted with his appearance that she said she would never read any of his poetry. Josephine states that she had just seen in the English newspaper that he has attacked her and her work 'in the most cruel and indecent manner'. Quotes from a letter she has received from James Stuart giving the impression the Sphinx has made upon him and comments: 'He has not much imagination, so it is something for him to be impressed'. A cipher telegram received from Charles at Ewart on Christmas Eve states: 'Delayed by cussedness of Vane's Company' [Charles went out to Western Australia in 1895]. 'Is Arthur [Bolton] with you just now?.. I hope Frank Hudson will soon get settled. It is hard for poor Con'. Con was Constance Hudson Arthur's sister.
title: Josephine Butler to Rhoda Butler

description: Folio 20. Stepney to Paget [believed to have arrived at the Porte]. Since he, Stepney, is uncertain whether Shrewsbury has a copy of Nottingham's cipher for correspondence with the chiefs of English missions, he will use the cipher Shrewsbury left with Bruynincx 'for the conveyance of news.. to the prejudice of the Allies and write at length what is against the French King'. The three weeks' siege of Castle Rheinfels, belonging to a Roman Catholic prince of the house of Hessen [Landgrave Ernest of Hessen-Rheinfels] by the French has been warded off by the intervention of the combined forces of Brandenburg: the French left exhausted and in disarray, having lost eighty officers and about 5,000 men. This may have some 'good effect' in Turkey. The elector of Brandenburg has, through his envoy at Vienna, solicited the Emperor that an express might be sent to Paget and Bruynincx. Stepney has obtained a copy of it from Strattmann. 'In all appearance this enterprize [siege of Rheinfels] which might have exposed the circles of Swabia and Franconia to new French assaults, was concerted with the Turks who expected great advantage by that diversion'. Operations in Flanders are not successful. Count Hoorn, governor of Furnes [West Belgium] has surrendered the place without striking, Dixmuide has surrendered. The French will not 'magnify' these setbacks as great conquests though, in truth, these places only served to cover Nieupoort as an advanced post if the Allies intended to attack Dunkirk towards the opening of the campaign.- Latest news: voting by Parliament of five millions for the maintenance of 33,000 seamen and more than 54,000 land forces; disputes between Nottingham and Admiral Russell [later Lord Orford, for not completing destruction of French navy]; margrave Louis of Baden's taking command on the Upper Rhine and his hoped-for forces; elevation of the duke of Hanover to the ninth electorate; conference attended by Stepney and Bruynincx at the Emperor's behest (see f.10v); and resignation of general count [Antonio] Caraffa [commissary general for war] who is 'very severe' against cardinal count [Leopold] Kolonitsch [president of the Hungarian chamber]. The estates of the arch-duchy of Lower Austria met on Jan 2/12 at the imperial palace in the presence of the Emperor and count Strattmann to deliberate and to vote the Emperor subsidies for carrying on the war on two fronts, i.e. against the Turks and against France. The sum expected is said to be 250,000 rixdollars, a guess, 'since the chancellor [Strattmann], according to custom, delivered the Emperor's demand, with the particulars, in writing, sealed, into the hands of count [Otto] Traun, marshal [i.e. governor] of that province'. Cardinal Kolonitsch, as president of the administration of finances, is preparing an extensive reduction of revenue staff in the hereditary territories: of 60,000 employees, 42,000 are to stay. He has also undertaken to 'remonstrate to the Emperor that of 86,000 men [under arms] 'which he supposed he had in Hungary there were not above 35,000 effective', the commissaries' accounts having been found to be 'unreasonable'. Date and Place: 1693 Jan 30 Vienna.

context: Manuscripts.Carew Manuscript.
description: "Although her Majesty hath by her letters taken notice of your Lordship's wise and happy proceedings, by a letter which hath been sent from Dublin by the Treasurer, upon your taking of the island in Tyrone, yet we are moved to express our sympathy with your good fortune both out of duty to the public and particular affection to yourself, whom God hath made so happy an instrument of her Majesty's service. We have likewise heard from the President of Munster of his taking in of Berehaven, whereby we had well hoped that province would have proved less troublesome than yet we can hope. First, because there are many of the provincial rebels out; next, because [In cipher.] the hollowness of those that are reputed subjects appeareth many ways (though not so visible to all), which is only maintained by the assurance they have of succours from Spain, whereof (as we have often said) we can make no other judgment than that what he is able to do he hath a will to do, and what he hath not done hath only been hindered by the remaining of her Majesty's fleet upon his coast, and which she resolveth to maintain till winter be well come on. So as, seeing here is done as much as her Majesty can do, and that many difficulties at home with himself and actions of others abroad may make suspension if not diversion from that Spanish invasion, we think your Lordship shall do well to take time while it serveth in Ulster, seeing we perceive you have now so ordered the matter as if he should land in the North, you are near him, and if in the South, you have means now to draw most of the force of the kingdom to make head against him. "Now that her Majesty hath read both your letters and the President's.. she is fully acquainted to what both your practices tend with the Spaniards, and how you two deal one with another in intercepting each other's great presents; for, as you sent before by Sir Oliver St. John your own original letter and the copy of his, so hath he sent his, and withal a report from Captain Harvy of the speech between him and Pedro Sotto, whereof the passport proceeded which Pedro Sotto sent to Captain Harvy. Of all which formalities and compliments usual between such persons as you are that profess arms, as none of you two need have made excuses, so is there no cause to speak further than of toys which usually pass between great commanders, though greatest enemies; yet of this matter between these two inferior captains her Majesty thinketh it not amiss to make some overture, whereby to reap some service, and that in this sort following: "Where the Spaniard and Captain Harvye take the liberty of soldiers (though otherwise enemies) one to do other courtesies, it is determined that Harvye shall take occasion to write into Spain to the Veedor how sorry he is, in respect of the goodwill he bears him who is like to be employed, that ever the King should resolve to send him with any forces into Ireland, seeing how much he is abused by the rebels' reports of their strength, and of the success of her Majesty's affairs against the rebels; who, if they were in bad case when he was there, they were much worse now. By occasion whereof he shall write of all particulars tending to that purpose of showing the good successes of her Majesty's army; wherein he shall pretend to be the more willing to discharge that good office, because he hath so good an evidence how the rebels abuse the King his master, namely, in O'Donnell's writing according to this copy, whereof the President hath the original, which he shall warrant Captain Harvye to send to him. In all which courses if it shall be said that all this will be thought but a device, sure we are, if there be nothing gotten there shall be nothing lost. "But that which is most hereby intended is this, that under this colour some carvill may be sent to that coast, and some man wiser than other, who may bring true relation of all such preparations as are made at the Groyne, where the greatest part of that force which is intended for Ireland will be drawn to a head. Thus have you all that we have cause to write at this time, whereof we were willing to take any occasion, especially having so good a subject whereof to congratulate, though there be no necessity of any other directions." Court at Greenwich, 18 July 1602. Signed by the "Lord Keeper, Lord Admiral, Sir Ro. Cecyll, Sir J. Fortescue." P.S. (in cipher).--"Although we find your Lordship had very good reason to draw away Sir Sam. Bagenall with those extraordinary companies which you were content to spare till the taking of the Castle of Donboy, yet we have thought it very convenient, because it is worth your Lordship's knowledge, to let you understand that if the Spaniards shall attempt to land in Ireland with an army, all our intelligences do confirm that it will be in Munster, or upon the nearer parts of Connaught; and, if this summer at all, it will be between this and Bartholomew tide. In which respect we thought it good to remember your Lordship to have some care for a month or two to send some forces to strengthen that province above the list; whereby at their first descent her Majesty's forces may keep such reputation, as the provincials, whose eye will only be upon the army, may not grow too insolent, nor the governor there be forced to leave the field. For which purpose we think it not amiss that you should presently send some horse, though you spare the fewer foot, considering the weakness of those numbers that are there to answer any such occasion. For the North, although we doubt not but O'Donnell is fed with the same hopes that the Munster rebels are, yet we do not expect any great forces to land in those parts more northerly than the town of Gallwaye at the furthest, if so it be." Copy. The parts in cipher are deciphered by Carew on a separate sheet. [The cipher is the same simple one as that used in Mountjoy's letters to Carew.] Endorsed by Carew: Received in my L. Deputy's letter the 5 of August 1602, which letter bare date the 1st of August.
title: THE PRIVY COUNCIL to the LORD DEPUTY MOUNTJOY.
