description: Concerning the 100l. given to you, which the two Justices interpret to be prejudicial to them, the warrant declares that over and above the fee of 100l. due to the Chief Justice, this reward of 100l. extra is appointed to him that should be of English birth. I did not mean to abridge the allowance of the Justices, but I have made the warrant to Mr. Treasurer more plain. Advertise in cipher what rebels remain in those parts, and where their haunt is. If you have a pledge upon Sir Owen McCartie, I allow of his departure home. Proceed to the arraignment of Sir James of Desmond, but forbear the execution until you hear more from me. Asketten, 15 August 1580. Signed. Concerning Sir John of Desmond's request to have conference with you, I authorize you thereto. If he will deliver his brother the Earl, Doctor Sanders, and the Seneschal [of Imokilly], you may grant him life. Have great regard lest this device be but a practice to make you a pledge to counterpoise Sir James. If Sir John, upon assurance of his life only, will not be drawn to deliver the foresaid parties, then may you grant him pardon of life, lands, and goods. As the Seneschal is in those parts, you may either draw towards Sir John with your forces to parley with him, or else bend your course into these parts. Let the Countess of Clancare be carefully looked unto, and demand of her for the young lady, the Earl of Desmond's daughter, which should have been brought thither with her. 15 August 1580. Dutch wish the King of Spain to execute the Act of Neutrality of the Empire. The Bishop of Münster is making every effort to persuade the Emperor and his ministers to demand the restoration of all formerly Imperial towns conquered by the Spaniards and currently possessed by the Dutch. Sudden lifting of siege and retreat by the Imperial troops from Canissa attributed to discord amongst generals and negligence. Date and place: 1660 June 21 [OS or NS] Leeuwarden.

context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Holland. Correspondence and papers of the Secretary of State: Holland (described at item level).
description: Folio 96: De Bacquoy to Bennet. Dutch send two special envoys to Sweden and to Denmark to try and persuade them to honour their treaty obligations. Dutch military preparations. Hope the English sailors will be tired by having been at sea so long. Ships carrying masts from Sweden together with the English ambassador, Carlisle, had to return to port because of contrary winds, and then became iced in. Harsh weather delays Dutch ship construction. Dutch forbid sale of newly constructed ships abroad. De Witt is seeking a declaration from the Provinces that due to the aggressions of the English, war may be inevitable and taxes and preparations are inevitable; this may be to protect him from public wrath in the future. English and Scottish mercenaries to be replaced by Dutchmen recruited by the several Provinces. New taxes to include one on each chimney, and a tax on inter-Province travel. Loans to be raised. Description of English fleet which has entered Spithead after patrolling the Channel. Secret letters from England allege that the English will not accept French mediation. Cominges has asked French merchants not to claim their vessels themselves, but allow him to prepare a `libel' for presentation to the English, since war has not been declared. description: Folio 110v. Stepney to Paget. Compares what has so far reached the English government from Heemskerck with 'other letters' received at Vienna from Turkey. Whilst Heemskerck, though not altogether without hope of an eventual peace, has 'greatly magnified' Turkish preparations for war, Paget, as appears from information imparted to him, Stepney, by Marco Antonio, the interpreter, emphasised his role as an 'ordinary ambassador.. to protect the English nation and to entertain the good friendship.. betwixt the Turks and Us without making any proposition out of season', for which he is 'much commended'. Heemskerck is 'much censured for pressing importunately and almost begging for a peace when the season was not favourable for such a proposition'. It appears that the Austrian ministers, though not expressing themselves, wish in their hearts that Heemskerck had never gone, his hopes were just 'idle notions'. Encloses, for news from all parts, a lengthy summary of events, based on extracts of 'all my letters and intelligence' which is to inform Paget on 'the state of Europe' and draws his attention to a 'little pamphlet call'd Lettre Historique' printed in Holland monthly which he will forward with his own letters via Transylvania, with a duplicate via Venice to be sent to Smyrna. Has asked Warre to send him a key of Paget's cipher with Nottingham. Meanwhile Paget may care to use the invisible ink 'which Mr Beintema [Unidentified] gave to Mr Heemskerke'. He [Beintema] 'will give me the secrett to understand'. If Paget's letters to Whitehall are to pass Vienna, 'you may send them with a flying seal (as Mr Heemskerke does his) which will save you the trouble of copying'. Enclosure: Headed 'London'. Date and Place: 1693 Mar 22 Vienna.

description: Folio 105: Wickfort to [Williamson]. 'La Hage, ce 3 mai, de Wickfort. Nous avons ici le traité de nos ambassadeurs. Il nous fut envoyé par un exprès dimanche dernier et a l'heure même on assemble aux états. La satisfaction que l'on en a est d'autant plus grande quel'on voit les Anglais reculés, en sorte que les ambassadeurs par leurs dernières lettres demandent permission de revenir parce que leurs commissaires forment tous les jours de nouvelles difficultés et qu'en l'absence du roi et pendant les cérémonies du mariage et de l'entrée de la reine, ils ne pourront rien negocier. Je ne sais ce qu'on resoudra la-dessus, pour[tant] je ne crois pas qu'on les fasse revenir. Le roi d'Angleterre s'est déclaré et a refusé d'entrer dans le traité que l'on vient de conclure en France, s'accusant sur ce qu'il est à la veille de conclure avec cet état, en sorte qu'il [n'a] pas besoin qu'il se fasse comprendre dans l'autre. Les ministres d'Autriche sont au désespoir de la conclusion de ce traité par[ce] qu'ils voient bien qu'ils n'en feront pas avec cette république. C'est pourquoi [ ] leurs pensées vont a obliger l'Empereur à s'accommoder avec le Turc et le roi d'Espagne avec les Portugais que je crois que l'un et l'autre se fera, a moins que les Espagnols fassent de grands progrès cette année en Portugal à quoi il n'y a pas beaucoup d'apparence?. Date and place: 1662 May 3 Hague.

description: Instructions given him by the Lord Justice and Council at Dublin the 13th of January 1579. Make sail along the west and north-west sea coasts, for the pursuit, apprehending, and plaguing of any traitors or malefactors adherent to the proclaimed traitors Gerald, Earl of Desmond, John and James his brethren, and all such as come to their aid or go from them with messages or letters. Address yourself to meet with Gilbert Yorke, captain of The Achates, now on the west coasts. Watch and keep the channels of the west harbours and coasts clear and free from annoyance of any foreign enemies, and apprehend all pirates. Repair to the island of Ineskethie on the river of Shenen, that you may receive there intelligence from us, the Lord Justice, upon our repair to Limerick, how you shall be then directed. Search all ships in the said west or north-west parts of the realm; seize all prohibited wares; "search all passengers for letters, books, ciphers, or other kind of suspect matter, that may tend either to the defacing of religion or to the dishonour of the Queen's most excellent Majesty, or any practice against this realm and State;" and commit to safe guard and custody all suspected or culpable persons. Make stay of any English, French, Spanish, Flemish, or Scottish ships, laden with any kind of victuals, and convoy them into the Shenen. We will take order, upon our coming to Limerick, for the discharge and payment of the same victuals. Any ships freighted or bargained for by any merchants of Dublin, Drogheda, Waterford, Cork, or any other corporate towns, shall be suffered to pass. Signed by the Deputy and Council. Contemp. copy.
title: GEORGE THORNTON, Captain of The Handmaid.

description: Folio 63. To Bruynincx. [Salutation 'Mon cher amy']. Has been travelling about [in Saxony] and visited the tombs of late electors at Freiberg and the electoral silver mines [there]. Does not think Boineburg will return. Wonders what made them [Vienna] choose the young count [Alois Thomas Raimund] Harrach as envoy to Saxony [He arrived at Dresden on Sept 4 1694 and stayed there until the end of April 1696]. As Bruynincx has Paget's cipher, he, Stepney, entreats him to inform him 'touchant les disgraces des chambellans du Roy des Romains [Joseph, later emperor Joseph I], parmy le nombre de quels il me semble qu'il est apparement qui'ls ont appris à Sa jeune Maj[es]té à f. ou à branler la pique, ce qui ne convient pas à l'austerité de la maison d'Autriche'. Schöning has arrived 'this evening' and was received at the frontier. Speculates on the effect of his return. All Saxon privy councillors are against him. Refers to his meeting with 'le fameux admiral de Danube [Assemburg] who was one of his party at Freiberg. Lexington is still with the army [in Flanders]. Should he pass through Dresden, he, Stepney, will endeavour to make him seek Bruynincx's friendship. It can only be to his advantage 'de trouver à son arrivée à Vienna la connoissance d'une personne qui connoit l'air du bureau comme vous le connoissez'. Mentions the ratifications having been bungled-up by 'messieurs de notre chauellerie'. Whether the elector will go to the army on the Rhine is uncertain: he may stay at home, hunting or seeking diversion 'avec des grivoises'. Reference to the disappearance of Königsmarck. Paget has written to Blathwayt in order to move the King to permit Stepney an excursion to Turkey. Date and Place: 1694 Aug 10/20 Dresden.

description: Folio 13: [Chauran] to [Williamson ]. `Ma lettre que je vous écrivis le 11 est demeurée par la faute de mes gens. Comme elle ne contient rien, je ne vous l'envoye pas. Rendez cette lettre marquée # a l'homme qui vous aura rendu plusieurs dépêches, et voyez ce que je lui ai mandé. Voici un abrégé de ce que l'on mande de Londres du 9 janvier: il y a eu querelle entre la Duchesse de York et la Duchesse de Richmond la dernière ayant dit des parolles fort offensentées et la qualifiant de Maitresse Hyde ce que le roi ayant su, il les a accommodées. Le Comte de St. Albans a fait festir au roi, et fort splendide, ce neantmoins il n'est pris de bon part a raison qu'il y a paru du dessein et de l'affectation. [ ] et sa femme font sous main ce qu'ils peuvent, le [ ], et son[t] aisement persuadés qu'il est souhaitable d'être les maîtres, a quoi les presbytériens contribuent, non pour le bien qu'ils leurs souhaitent, mais pour brouiller les cartes. Le chiffre on est des barres dessous est de celui qui écrit, l'on ne sait pas encore son nom et change tous les jours d'écriture et d'addresse. Je crois qu'il veut parler du Comte de Manchester Les barres a mon chiffre signifie les quantiesme que Mr. Nicholas fasse si bien en sorte que Milord Hyde s[o]it d'accord de tout et qu'il ne puisse prendre aucun ombrage de ceci. Adieu. J'attends le succès de toute chose. Si cela ne réussit point et que le roi ne donne rien'. Payment of couriers; changes in postal arrangements.

description: Folio 138. To Paget. He has urged Shrewsbury and Blathwayt to send Lexington to Vienna 'out of hand'. Speculates, on the basis of certain correspondence received by him, on the disposition of the Porte to treat of peace in the face of a possible, and more determined, intervention by Poland. Has it from one source that Vienna is planning to send counts [Charles Ernest] Waldstein and [Hermann Jacob] Czernin as well as [the cavaliere] Alessandro Zeno [Zen], Venetian ambassador at Vienna, to a peace congress at Strij. No news of Heemskerck having reached Belgrade as yet. - His business at Dresden is unfinished due to the 'fatality' of the elector's death. Of his brother and successor Frederick Augustus, he 'cannot say much good'. The body of countess Rochlitz has been 'dug up and used with as much barbarity as any is practis'd in the countries where you are'. The new elector is too busy to think of the campaign and has put his father-in-law, the margrave [Ernest Christian] of Bayreuth in charge of the army with count [Henry VI] Reuss, promoted 'Feld-zeugmeister' [i.e. general of artillery] as his deputy. Schöning will, after all, be released, but the new elector has given an undertaking not to employ him in any military or civilian capacity. - Continues his chronicle of events in England, giving detailed account of changes in the peerage, in the treasury - Montague having been appointed under-treasurer and chancellor of the exchequer - and in the admiralty. - Margrave Louis of Baden had ordered a rendez-vous of all confederate troops at Heilbronn on May 7/17, but without the Saxons as yet. No surprise attack by the French is anticipated. [First para interspersed with cipher]. Date and Place: 1694 May 22 O.S. Dresden.

description: Folio 18: De Bacquoy to [Williamson]. Indication that Louis XIV hopes to mediate between England and the United Provinces; Dutch pleased to learn that Admiral Montague's ship is undermanned and the crew complain they have not been paid and lack victuals; Dutch plan to send spies to learn of British preparations and plans. Sweden and Denmark prepare for possibility of war. Zealand has asked that her garrisons be reinforced and that some musketeers be withdrawn from the frontier and redeployed on her warships. Gogh leaves for England with instructions to gather intelligence. Dutch receive a report that English naval preparations seem to have halted, and various ministers, like Downing, would prefer an accommodation to a war; however English subjects abroad have been ordered to return home and travelling abroad has been forbidden. Dutch arrange to meet and escort home their East Indies fleet. Other naval preparations are being made discreetly and Dutch warships are not putting to sea to avoid an accidental starting of the war or provoking an English attack. Dutch wish that England should reveal herself to France and other countries as the aggressor if war should break out. Dutch negotiation with Portugal over Cochin and Cananor and with Denmark over disputes in West Africa. Provinces asked to pay a special contribution for additional warships and crews. Brandenburg demands that Dutch settle the Hoef-ÿsser debt. French troops sent to [assist the Emperor] are to be taught German, dictionaries are to be distributed amongst the officers in the hope that by overcoming language barriers the French and German troops can be brought to an harmonie compatible. Turks vanquish imperial army at Canissa. States General are very angry to hear that the English have seized Cape Verde and three Dutch West Indies vessels, directly contrary to Charles II's promises. Date and place: 1660 June 14 [OS or NS] [Leeuwarden].
title: Folio 18: De Bacquoy to [Williamson]. Indication that Louis XIV hopes to mediate between England...

description: Folio 14: De Bacquoy to Bennet. Dutch dismay that the French seem to have decided not to help them. Zeeland pressing for letters of marque to be issued. Admiralties of Holland complain that only they are fulfilling their quota, and that the United Provinces are thus in peril from the English threat. Dutch might attack English ships and possessions in the East Indies and India; this has occasioned a sharp fall in the English East India Company's shares. Dutch will propose to the French that a mutual restitution of former possessions be made with England. Also Van Beuningen will show an Act authorising seizure of Dutch vessels and property, which should be proof to the French that England has commenced open hostilies against them and that French treaty obligation should now be honoured. Many Dutchmen angry that De Witt sent De Ruyter to Guinea secretly, without first obtaining the assent of the States General. De Witt's power. De Witt and his party are very apprehensive about the possibility of the English blockading the Dutch warships so that they cannot join up into a strong unified naval force. Dutch finding shortage of finance a serious obstacle to their planned naval expansion. The States General can only continue to urge the Provinces to try and fulfil their quotas. Friesland has proposed that the East Indies Company should be made to contribute towards the costs since they have made substantial profits and [are the main cause of the present emergency]. To conciliate France the States General have ordered those deputies `responsible for the affairs of Malta' to find means of inducing Guelders to satisfy the demands of the Grand Master of Malta. The Empire might not intervene to defend the Spanish Netherlands for fear of provoking conflict with France. Dutch apprehensive about war preparations being made by the Bishop of Münster. Date and place: 1665 Jan 10 [OS or NS] [Leeuwarden].

description: Folio 82. Stepney to Blathwayt. Encloses a copy of Paget's letter which came in Veterani's packet for Kinsky, to whom he, Stepney, gave a translation of Paget's dispatch, omitting, however, the passages concerning Heemskerck and margrave Louis. Analyses Kinsky's antogonism to both ambassadors to the Porte and thinks that 'when the great work [i.e. peace] is done (which chiefly supports his credit at this court)', Kinsky may be regarded as a 'superannuated minister', Strattmann having 'outed' him already in most affairs. Observes that the present negotiation ought never to have been entrusted to two ambassadors 'who seem to quarrell for the prize before they are in any likelihood of catching it.. under the direction of a minister who is at enmity with them both'. Peace must needs ensue if the 'Imperialists gain any advantage this summer: Kinsky suspects that the grand vizier will take Heemskerck along with him to have him at hand as a mediator in case of any misfortune. The imperial army has moved towards Peterwardein and the Turks expect them to assault Temesvar rather than Belgrade. Mentions a sharp dispute between the Emperor and the Pope whose archers have recently ill-treated some personnel of the Emperor's ambassador at Rome which the Emperor's Heyducks afterwards 'revenged on the Popes officers', the breach is not yet disposed of. D'Hervart has written him that he had received notice from England that the time was not yet 'ripe' for the use of a transit passport for the Swiss refugees to be transported to Ireland, on whose behalf he, Stepney, had recently presented a memorial to the Emperor. Encloses copies of the intercepted letters referred to in his dispatch of July 12/22 (see f.79). The Emperor's clerks have not been able to break the cipher in its entirety. Date and Place: 1693 July 15/25 Vienna.

context: Secretaries of State: State Papers Foreign, Russia. Details of this piece are described at item level.
description: Folio 167: Whitworth to Harley. Difficulties with the post and various expedients to remedy it. Goodfellow's desire to return to England and the opinion of the Russia Company on his return. Goodfellow's difficulties: necessity for his successor to be appointed. Whitworth's cold reception by the Czar when he wished to discuss the merchants' grievances. Whitworth feels the Czar and his `Favourite' are hostile to the Russia Company's aims. Possibility of the Czar's entering the Grand Alliance, and the wisdom of the creation of a treaty of commerce with Russia. Whitworth feels the Czar's advisers intend to use a treaty for self-interested purposes, or have no intention of bringing the negotiation to fruition. Encloses copy of his letter to Shapfiroff (f. 176). Confused reports from Lithuania. Merchants on their way to England met Prince Menschikoff in disorderly retreat. Arrival of the Prussian envoy with confirmation of confusion amongst the Russians. Czar's movements. Crown army still supports Czar, but widespread rumours of Augustus' claims to crown of Poland seem to have been unfounded. Details of these rumours and their sources. Information deduced from the Russians' movements about General Loewenhaupt and his army. Removal of Swedish inhabitants from Dorpt. Arrival of eminent Swedish prisoners sent to Stockholm on parole. Archbishop of Lemberg forced to return to Moscow because of military activities. Progress of the fortifications of Moscow; doubt whether they will stand firm when the weather breaks. Arms which will be mounted on the fortifications. Histories of le Mestre de Sault, a Walloon and inventor of artillery, and of Fox, an Englishman engaged in work for the Czar. Birthday of the hereditary prince. Troops ordered to Viasma. Rebellion of the Baskirsky Tartars, and their previous harsh treatment by the Prebolskiks. Restoration of their previous governor, with promises to examine their grievances. Presence of large numbers of Muscovite troops. Dated Moscow, 10/21 Mar 1708. Partly in cipher.
title: Folio 167: Whitworth to Harley. Difficulties with the post and various expedients to remedy it....

description: Letter of W[illiam] W[ynn] W[estcott], 396 Camden Road, London N to an unknown correspondent [?Percy Bullock, a solicitor}, marked Private and Confidential, returning draft High Council notice about The Equinox case, in which Aleister Crowley published the Golden Dawn rituals. Westcott asks the recipient to omit item 3, which was read at a Special Council meeting. Westcott hopes all goes well at the meeting in Sheffield and asks if the proof notice has been received from them. Will leave a copy of The Equinox magazine number 3 at the recipient's house to read the attack on Westcott by Crowley based on details given by a swindler [ie Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers]. Westcott mentions he had declarations witnessed by two individuals ten years before that he had received and answered correspondence from S.D.A [Sapiens Dominabitur Astris aka Fraülein Sprengel] in Germany. At the time Crowley accepted the veracity of the letters and Westcott suggests using 'every smooth means first' to obtain a retraction. Suggests the recipient writes notes dated the present date and also one dated about 23 December ten years earlier. Mentions that H[oros] was convicted on 20 December, while M[athers] was in Paris. After slanderous remarks about Westcott made ten years before, [Mathers] signed an agreement not to speak so again before the Horos trial. Westcott mentions he has two letters dated 1886 to 1887 from [Mathers]concerning the Cipher MSS of the Rev A F A Woodford, from which [Mathers] hoped to write up new rituals of the Golden Dawn ritual Grades 0 = 4. Westcott also mentions a letter from M[athers] from Bradford, Yorkshire, in which Mathers informs Westcott that he has told [Thomas Henry] Pattinson about Westcott's correspondence with S.D.A. Westcott informs the recipient that he will give [Mathers] five pounds if he will do what Westcott wants but not to make it look like bribery.
title: Letter of William Wynn Westcott to an unknown correspondent

description: The file is about a change in administrative arrangements, following receipt of a general instruction in 1939, to send all future intelligence summaries to the new Middle East Intelligence Centre (M.E.I.C.) at Cairo. The file contains confidential, secret and most secret copy letters and telegrams, mainly from Trenchard Craven William Fowle (Political Resident in the Persian Gulf) to the Political Agent, Bahrain. The correspondence begins with a request from Fowle, asking the Political Agent, Bahrain to start sending copies of his fortnightly intelligence summaries to the newly opened M.E.I.C. Both this request and subsequent correspondence contains detailed instructions about the secure communication of intelligence reports and summaries between British officials in the Arab Gulf States and the Intelligence Centre at Cairo, including the use of cyphers and code words. The copy correspondence includes a secret telegram (T. No. 9276 dated 19 April 1941) and a most secret memorandum ( M.E.I.C./1/59 dated 21 April 1941) from the Intelligence Centre, containing instructions about the use of the code word 'Steel' in messages to indicate that information has been supplied by a most secret source (ff.13-17). The file also includes copies of six printed distribution lists with the security classification 'Most Secret', for the circulation of intelligence summaries compiled by the Political Intelligence Centre Middle East, May-June 1943.
title: 'File 4/2 (1.a/50) M.E.I.C. publicity'.

description: Folio 151. To Trenchard. Has returned with Ham from Leipzig and they have, on the basis of what they have been able to ascertain, discussed three trends in electoral policy which are likely to surface in the near future. The first concerns Schöning's future. In this connection, he describes the shady dealings of Holtzbrinck, the elector's personal special agent, who, though he has as yet not very far progressed, was to be reckoned with on account of his close relationship with the elector despite of being 'a person of an obscure and mean figure' and, in fact, a Brandenburg subject, working outside the electoral chancery, and disavowed by the other Saxon diplomats, is accredited to the imperial court. His business is bribery: he is equipped with 100,000 rixdollars, and one imperial minister, 'who is poor and lives high' is suspected of having succumbed to temptations [Cipher '1433' (?Königsegg)], whilst others 'are not capable of being corrupted'. According to Ham, to use a Brandenburg subject on behalf of Schöning would be 'diametrically opposite' to the elector of Brandenburg's resolution not to concern himself in Schöning's interest. - The second 'point' likely to emerge is the elector's project, already 'positively agreed to' by the political estates [in the regional diet assembled] of a new levy of five regiments, obviously to increase subsidies from the allied powers. Both Ham and Stepney have agreed to cut short the delay this new proposition was bound to entail for the business in hand, namely the Grand alliance, and 'take little notice of such an overture'. - The third 'point' is that the elector 'would willingly draw the Emperor to befriend him in his pretensions to Saxe-Lawemburgh' and would engage the King and the States to assist by their good offices. 'To which the Emperor answers: The law lyes open'. Ham and Stepney shall decline to be concerned in this business 'which does not concern us & which can naturally have no place in the treaty'. - Notifies him of his counsultation with Stratford about payment of the outstanding 50,000 rixdollars subsidies due at this time.

adminHistory: Charles Vernon Somers Cocks was born at 13 Montagu Place, Marylebone, London on 1st June 1895 to parents Thomas Somers Vernon Cocks and Ethel Mary Fellowes. His father was a partner in the family banking firm of Cocks, Biddulph & Co. of London which was founded in 1757. In 1913, Charles left Eton to study at Christ Church, Oxford. He was appointed as a 2nd Lieutenant to a Special Reserve Commission in The Black Watch, with effect from 27th December 1914. He was to report to the 3rd Battalion at Nigg Camp, Ross-shire, Scotland. On 6th October 1915, Charles joined the 2nd Battalion at Givenchy and was promoted to Lieutenant on the 18th. He proceeded to Mesopotamia (Modern day Iraq) with the Battalion, when the India Corps was sent to attempt the relief of Kut-al-Amara, being in command of No. 10 Platoon of No. 3 Company. On 7th January 1916, Charles was wounded in the left arm at Shaikh Sa’ad and on the 16th January, he was evacuated to hospital in Bombay. He permanently lost the use of his arm. In March 1916, he returned to England by a hospital ship for further treatment and six months leave. He was seconded to the War Office, where he worked in the cipher room until after the end of the war, being discharged with the rank of Captain, to which he had been promoted on the 19th November 1917. In March 1918, Charles married Genifer Gaunt. After his military career, he joined the family bank of Cocks, Biddulph & Co. which had been taken over by the Liverpool & Martins Bank. He worked there until after his father’s death. In 1934, he went to live at Chagford, Devon, where he remained for the rest of his life and died on 16th September 1977.

adminHistory: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn was founded in 1888 by Dr William Wynn Westcott, Dr William Robert Woodman, and Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers who were all Freemasons and members of Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia (S.R.I.A.). The Order was based on the rituals and knowledge lectures found in the Cipher Documents. [A series of encrypted documents containing outlines for a series of initiation rituals, see GBR 1991 GD 1/1/1-8]. Although the history and authenticity of these documents has been greatly debated it is now generally agreed that they were written by Kenneth Mackenzie as outline rituals for the Society of Eight [a Golden Dawn prototype founded by Frederick Holland in 1883 which never fully manifested] or the Sat B’hai [This Order, founded around 1871 by Captain J H Lawrence-Archer, using vaguely Hindu terminology within a framework derived from Masonry, it seemed to have had little more than a paper existence until 1875 when Mackenzie joined.] On Mackenzie’s death, Westcott acquired these papers and set about transferring them into full grade rituals. An additional paper found within the cipher documents contained the address of a woman in Germany referred to as Fraülein Sprengel. Described as being an Adept of an occult order known as the Die Goldene Dämmerung, Westcott asserted that she had authorized him through a series of letters to set up a Temple in England, with permission to sign her name. Many researchers now believe that Westcott created this story in order to give the Golden Dawn a legitimate pedigree and attract serious occultists and freemasons to his new order. The Order grew steadily and by the end of 1888 there were three temples, Isis-Urania in London, Osiris in Weston-Super-Mare and Horus in Bradford. From 1888 to 1891 the Golden Dawn functioned as a theoretical school, performing the initiation ceremonies of the Outer Order from the 0°=0° Neophyte grade to the 4°=7° Philosophus grade and teaching the basics of the Qabalah, astrology, alchemical symbolism, geomancy and tarot. No practical magic was performed until 1891, when Mathers completed the ritual for the 5°=6° grade, the first grade of the Secord or Inner Order of the Golden Dawn, known as the Order of the Rosae Rubeae et Aureae Crucis (the Ruby Rose and Cross of Gold). By this time Woodman had died and as a replacement was not appointed, Mathers managed to reconstruct the Order, becoming its primary Chief. The new 5=6 ritual was based on the legend of Christian Rosenkreuz, a great spiritual teacher who was secretly buried and later found perfectly preserved within a seven sided tomb. Mathers and his wife Moina (nee Mina Bergson) created an elaborate full-size version of his tomb, referred to as the Vault of the Adepts, which members of the Inner Order used when performing the rituals. The Inner Order put theory into practice with members making and consecrating their own magical implements. Mathers also created a formal curriculum, which included guidance on scrying, astral travel and alchemy, with a series of eight graded examinations which lead to members achieving the sub-grade of Theoricus Adeptus Minor. The Order continued to grow and two further temples were opened in 1893, Amen-Ra in Edinburgh, Scotland and the Ahathoor Temple, Paris, to where Mathers had relocated in 1892. In 1895 the stability of the Order was threatened by the breakdown of the relationship between Mathers and his sponsor, Annie Horniman. This lead to her expulsion and increasing unrest among Second Order Adepts in London. In 1897 further problems arose when civil authorities became aware of Westcott’s link with the group, forcing him to resign in order to keep his position as Coroner for North East London. Florence Farr assumed Westcott’s role but without his administrative support, the reduced supervision of grade work and the examination system undertaken by members in London led to further decline of the Order. By 1900 Mathers’ domineering behaviour led to Farr suggesting that the Order should be dissolved. Fearing this was an attempt to replace him with Westcott, Mathers wrote to Farr stating that Westcott had forged the Sprengel letters. As Westcott declined to defend himself this shook the trust of London members in particular, leading to open rebellion after Mathers initiated Aleister Crowley, who had been refused admission as a member in the London Temple. A committee was set up to investigate Mathers’ claims which led to the expulsion of Mathers, Moina Mathers, Crowley and other supporters in May 1900, despite Mathers sending Crowley as his envoy to London in an attempt to take possession of the Inner Order headquarters at 36 Blythe Road, London (subsequently referred to as the Battle of Blythe Road). Supporters loyal to Mathers formed a rival Isis Temple, headed by Mathers and run by Dr Edward Berridge, later known as Alpha and Omega 1. The Paris Temple and later Amen-Ra in Edinburgh, under the guidance of John W. Brodie-Innes, also became part of Mather’s Alpha and Omega Order. After Mathers’ displacement, William Butler Yeats took over the Temple in London. The reinstatement of Annie Horniman, who led disputes over the forgotten examination system and Farr’s splinter organisation, known as the Sphere Group, led to further concerns. Such troubles were exacerbated in 1901, following unwanted publicity arising from the Horos case. An American couple, Frank and Editha Jackson, also known as Theo and Laura Horos, used the rituals, which they had duped Mathers into handing over to them in Paris, to set up their own order in London, known as the Order of Theocratic Unity. They defrauded and raped several young women persuaded to join this Order and the subsequent court case lead to the exposure of many Golden Dawn secrets in the press. Editha Jackson was also known as the Swami Vive Ananda and assumed various other names, including Anne O'Delia Diss De Bar but was born into a respectable Kentucky family, the Salomons, during a criminal career as a spiritualist and extortionist in New York and New Orleans, America. As a result of this Case, leading to the imprisonment of the American couple in London, many members left in order to distance themselves from the Golden Dawn. Remaining members changed the Order’s name to the Hermetic Society of the Morgenröthe. In 1903 a further schism occurred within the Order. Arthur Edward Waite took over the remnant of the original Isis-Urania Temple which became known as the Independent and Rectified Rite. Waite’s new Order moved away from the ritual magic present in the old Order, replacing it with a more mystical path. This Order existed until 1914 when internal disputes led to Waite closing the Temple and forming the Fellowship of the Rosy Cross in 1915. This existed until Waite’s death in 1942. Those members who preferred the rituals and magic developed by Mathers joined Dr Robert Felkin in his new organisation known as the Stella Matutina. Their temple, based in London was named Amoun. After lengthy negotiations, Felkin signed a concordat with Waite in 1907 to govern the relationship between the two Temples, but this agreement only lasted until 1910. Once he became Chief, Dr Felkin communicated with several mystical individuals including the discarnate Arab teacher, Ara Ben Shemesh and the Sun Masters. Increasingly, Felkin became interested in establishing new links with the ‘Secret Chiefs’ and the original Rosicrucian societies in Germany, with which Westcott had claimed to have had links. Felkin’s quest led him on several continental trips where he met the Austrian philosopher and esotericist, Ruldolf Steiner (1861-1925) and claimed to have been given higher grades, the equivalent to 8=3 and 7=4 grades. In addition Felkin corresponded with Anne Sprengel, whom he was treating for cancer, whom he claimed was the niece of Fraülein Sprengel. While travelling in New Zealand with his family in 1912, Felkin founded a new Temple, Smaragdum Thalasses, at Havelock North, Hawkes Bay, New Zealand. Before his relocation to New Zealand in 1916, Felkin issued a new constitution for Stella Matutina, which included details for three daughter temples for Amoun, namely Hermes Temple, Bristol (which became independent in the early 1920’s and survived until c. 1972); The Secret College, London, which was to be ‘confined to members of the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia, who have taken at least Grade 4’ (this college was active in 1921 but may not have survived long beyond this date0; and finally Merlin Temple, perhaps located in London but not established successfully, which was to consist of former members of Waite’s group or the Anthroposophical Society. After Felkin’s departure, the Order in London came under the control of Christina Mary Stoddart, who became increasingly paranoid and obsessed with details about the Order’s origins. After working for four years on her paper ‘Investigations into the Foundations of the Order G.D. and R.R. et A.C. and the Source of its Teachings’ she concluded that the whole Order was evil. Stoddart’s attitude, further internal disputes and bad publicity in the press led to the closure of the Amoun Temple, London, in the early 1920’s. By 1923 a significant quantity of the Order’s papers had been given by Stoddart to a colleague for safekeeping.

description: Contains records of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, its constituent and successor bodies and other related bodies [including Alpha et Omega, Stella Matutina, Independent and Rectified Rite, Fellowship of the Rosy Cross, Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia, Sphere Group, the Order of Great Osiris the Saviour, The Theosophical Society and others] The collection includes the original cipher manuscripts, later translations of the ciphers, additional ciphers, the ‘Sprengel’ letters, translation of the ‘Sprengel’ letters; ritual and instructional texts for both the Inner and Outer Orders in the Golden Dawn and its associated bodies, including grade ritual books, temple diagrams, Flying Rolls, lectures; National and Local administration and membership records including registers, address books, minutes, receipt and undertaking forms, Inner Order diaries, pledge forms, by-laws, circulars, correspondence and ephemera; personal correspondence of several prominent members including Florence Farr, Dr W Wynn Westcott, S.L. MacGregor Mathers, Annie Honiman, Rev William A. Ayton, Dr Robert Felkin and Christina Stoddart; case files relating to significant events within the Order’s history including the expulsion of Annie Horniman, the ‘Battle of Blyth Road, the Horos Case, the expulsion of Mathers, the dividing of the Order, the concordat between the Stella Matutina and the Independent and Rectified Rite, the Court Case between Mathers and Aleister Crowley over the publication of rituals in the Equinox, Felkin’s continental investigations and the Stella Matutina’s new constitution and daughter temples; regalia and artefacts including Rose Cross Lamens worn by the Inner order members, sashes, Enochian chess boards, Lotus wand, Westcott’s ring and disk used for divination, Enochian tablets, earth pentacle, officers’ wands, replica of the Inner Order Vault; photographs, designs and diagrams including temple diagrams, designs used in the vault; Garden of Eden after the fall of man, the colour scales, the minutum mundum; photographs including a picture of S. L. MacGregor Mathers; printed texts relating to the order including works by R.A. Gilbert, I Regardie and E Howe; and Robert Gilbert’s research papers.
title: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn and related bodies

description: Folio 213: Wickfort to [Williamson?]. `Paris [t]roi[s] mai, M.Wickfort. L'on a su par les lettres de Londres que les Anglais ont été fort touchés du traité et qu'ils avaient usé de menaces contre vos ambassadeurs, mais `unae sine viribus irae' et sans union. C'est pourquoi Messieurs les Etats Généraux se rendant forts en mer comme ils font par le nouveau armement de si grands vaisseaux. Ils n'ont rien à craindre, ayant (un?) alliance si etroite avec la France et avec garantie, mais pourvu qu'il n'y ait point de longueurs et d'accroche en la ratification comme il vous est arrivé avec le Portugal, tout ira bien et l'on doit faciliter toutes choses de part et d'autre. Je ne doute point que [Glasetle] ment l'Angleterre a cause de la garantie de la pêche, mais plus encore la maison d'Autriche, d'Espagne et d'Allemange n'ayont été touchés et comme au désespoir de la conclusion de ce traité qui co[n]tient, à ce que j'entends, Cinquante articles, que nous verrons avec (un?) peu de temps, voyant par lá leurs mesures rompus de pouvoir rétablir leur puissance, et par conséquent les ministres d'Autriche porteront leurs maîtres a faire la paix avec le Turc et la Portugal. L'on a su tout bessament qu'il a eu quel[que] proposition de mariage de Don Juan d'Autriche avec la princesse de Portugal pour rompre celui de l'angleterre et pour (?cemiecet). L'armée espagnole n'avait encore rien enterprise le 28 du passé, ni la flotte, qui essaie vers la coroni Aussi n'a-[t]-on point encore avis du départ de la dite princesse de Lisbone. Pour le Prince de Münster, je vous ai mandé ce qui s'est passé a la signature du traité. Je vous dirai maintenant de plus que les demandes et [les] affaires des princes alliées ayant été remises après la conclusion, c'est aussi à present que leurs résidents et agents se remuent plus jamais et tâchent d'obtenir de Sa Majeste que pour plus grande assurance des princes aliées, les paroles et les promesses des ambassadeurs se reduissent par ecrit avant qu'ils partent d'ici'. Date and place: 1662 May 5 Paris.

description: Folio 223. To Trenchard. Reports on the joint demarche, on Feb 25 O.S. by himself, Ham and Boineburg to Gersdorff and Knoch about the interception, opening and retention for several hours, of their diplomatic mail, of which they had conclusive evidence. Whilst theelector's regrets and explanation that he 'expressly' commanded Birckholtz and Rechenberg [gentleman-in-waiting] and secretary Beyer not to open the English and Dutch packets had to be noted, they take strongly exception and voice their indignation about having been victimised by the curiosity and malice of Birckholtz and Rechenberg, the former being a 'creature' of Schöning's, the latter his son-in-law 'and the person who 3 weeks ago had handed to the elector Holtzbrinck's malicious insinuations'. Moreover, both are suspected to be of the 'French faction', a matter of moment, since Stepney's packet 'accidently' contained 'letters of great consequence from Turkey'. Yet, though the elector's apologies and Gersdorff's arguments had no force, they agreed to attend at court as before, so as not to jeopardize any progress in their negotiations. Birckholtz's and Rechenberg's suspicions may have been heightened by their having some information that Carlowitz, now at Vienna, 'holds correspondence' with some persons at Dresden and works underhand against Schöning's interest at the imperial court. - Inserts, in cipher, secret information on excessively violent fits of temper suffered by the elector who attacked his mother, brother and consort, necessitating surgical intervention by blood-letting. - In conclusion, reports that Boineburg had, on the previous day, received the Emperor's resolution concerning Schöning's future. Schöning is to regain his full liberty on condition that the elector 'would no more employ him either in civill or military affaires till the war shall be at an end'. More than that the Emperor cannot grant 'without giving jealousyes to the allyes'. The elector, not entirely satisfied, will write to the Emperor again, but has told Stepney, Ham and Ilten that he will suspend sending his adjutant-general to Neidschütz, with orders to march his troops back to Saxony, until he has final advice from Vienna. Date and Place: 1694 Feb 27 O.S. Dresden.

description: Registry Number: AHQ/6507/SEC. Correspondence about the removal of works of art by Allied forces, dated 1945 - 1946. Note by the Secretariat of the Allied High Commission stating 'we have been asked by the Control Office to examine the whole question of unilateral removal of works of art from Germany, following on reports that the Soviets were removing works of art to Moscow, including some which were the property of non-Germans', dated May 1946. Correspondence between the Control Commission for Germany, the Control Office for Germany and Austria and the Secretariat in Berlin relating to the question of the disposal of works of art in Germany at quadripartite level and problems raised by the removal of art treasures by the Russians from their zone, dated April - May 1946. Copy of an article entitled 'German Paintings in the National Gallery: A Protest' from the American publication The College Art Journal , written by Mr Charles L Kuhn, late Lieutenant-Commander, US Navy, and now Professor of Fine Art at Harvard University, dated April 1946. Refers to the plan by the US Military Government to take German museum paintings to the US for 'safekeeping'. No reference to specific paintings. Control Commission correspondence about a loss of personal effects by Mr J A Thwaites, including paintings and sculptures, at Katowice, Poland, and enquiries made by the Art Commission in the Russian zone of Germany about this loss, dated March 1946. Control Commission correspondence relating to the scope of the Russian Art Commission, dated March 1946. Telegram from the Control Commission for Germany to Troopers stating that 'objects with British Royal associations are not such as can be used for replacement in kind of looted art treasures as they are all ornamented with cipher of George First, Second or Third or if pictures represent British Royal Family', date not readable. Correspondence between the Office of Military Government for Germany [US] and the Control Commission for Germany [British Element] relating to the removal of German works of art from the British zone, dated December 1945. Letter from Lieutenant General Lucius D Clay to Sir Brian H Robertson, Control Commission for Germany [British Element], about this matter, dated 7 December 1945. Includes List of 202 German works of art which have been sent to the United States 'for safe keeping in trust of the German people' [9 pages], undated. The List includes work by Van Eyck, Cranach, Lorenzetti, Holbein, Bruegel, Duerer, Botticelli, Rembrandt, De Hooch, Tiepolo, Rubens, Lippi, Titian, Vermeer, Velasquez and Raphael, amongst others. Press Release by the US State Department about the temporary removal from Germany to the United States of German art objects, dated October 1945. Includes related correspondence. No reference to specific works of art..

description: Folio 168. To Kinsky. Has failed to receive letters and duplicates [thereof] from Paget sent via Ragusa and via Transylvania, dated July 10/20 and 19/29, and July 24/Aug 3 and Aug 20/30, but has had a letter of Oct 2, 1693 from Pera di Constantinopoli which cameto Ragusa by an express and was sent by the Venetian consul to Venice and there handed to the English consul there [Broughton]. Gives contents of this letter which is entirely in cipher. Paget thinks it possible that the grand vizier, before being deposed, gave Castagnères written confirmation that Turkey would never make peace [with the Emperor]. He promises not to entertain any considerations by the Emperor towards Thököly. Nor has Heemskerck ever done so. He sharply criticizes Thököly's agents, count Sandor and Michael Inzidi, for their cunning and craftiness. Paget suggested to Inzidi that Thököly could only hope for English intercession for clemency if he turned his back on the Turks. Reports in some detail on French subsidies to Thököly. There was French and Turkish jubilation at the loss of the English merchant fleet and French successes on the Rhine and in Flanders and at the report that the Austrians had raised the siege of Belgrade which he refused to believe. Thinks that 1693 presented great opportunities to the Austrians since the Turkish army was ineffective, had not been paid, suffered from widespread desertion, and the [new] vizier was a weak man. Paget told the camaican [? of Adrianople] that England would spare no effort to persuade the Emperor to agree to a peace based on Uti possidetis, provided the Turks agreed to this beforehand. Yet, he has doubts about the prospects of a settlement leading to peace. He is unable to send more dispatches because of lack of facilities to expedite them. Letters cannot go by sea without French approval and there are difficulties in sending dispatches via Moldavia and Poland, or via Wallachia and Transylvania. Recommends that the pension paid by the Emperor to Janachiporforiti, agent of the prince of Transylvania, be renewed, as he was useful for forwarding dispatches. Expresses doubts about the reliability of Marsigli and Duval. The Arabs rebelled during 1693, and beat the army sent against them. Three months ago there were three fires in Constantinople which burnt down a third of the city, including grain and timber stores. Some few Turkish and Jewish individuals were induced to confess to arson and were hanged. Over a third of the population has died of the plague. News of the raising of the siege of Belgrade has quelled any Turkish inclination to enter peace negotiations. Date and Place: 1694 Jan 8/18 Dresden.

description: Correspondence between the Property Control branch of the Finance Division and the MFA and A branch of the I A and C Division relating to the investigation of the Bruns collection of Reformation medals 'of considerable historical value', kept, together with the contents of some of the largest German museums, at the Grasleben mine near Helmstedt, which was plundered in April 1945 and was currently being evacuated under MFA and A supervision, dated February 1946. Completed copy [in German] of the declaration of assets and obligations pursuant to Article II of Military Government Law No 53 on Foreign Exchange Control, filed in July 1945 by the Landesmuseum of Hannover for the collections of coins and medals originally owned by Herzog von Braunschweig and Lueneburg and currently kept at the Landesmuseum. Includes two copies of the English translation of the list of gold and silver coins kept at the Landesmuseum and the Welfenmuseum. Draft and final version of a cipher message from the British Element of the Control Commission for Germany in Berlin to the Chief of Staff on the subject of the restitution of works of art, undated. States that 'the great majority of works of art from enemy occupied territory now in the British Zone was acquired by purchase in the special exchange conditions of occupation. For the most part these purchases were made by Northern German museums [.], were extremely numerous and totalled many thousands of objects, representing very large sums of money.' Points out that if Sugra 18 [not specified, see FO 1046/147] 'is interpreted strictly, there will be very few works of art which can be returned to France, Belgium or Holland from the British Zone'. Records that 'pressure for return of such objects has been steady and is liable to increase. MFA and A branch are very anxious to proceed with practical work of restitution while their experienced personnel are still available' and urges that they 'proceed to effect interim restitution of these purchased works of art subject to a receipt'. Correspondence between the Banking branch, the Finance Division and the headquarters of the Military Government of the North Rhine region with attachments setting out dates and lists of blocked accounts belonging to the Reich, the German Armed Forces, the NSDAP, absent owners and remainders for a total of RM 1,153,465,235.94 as of July 1945, dated September-October 1945. Note by the Allied Secretariat on interim restitution deliveries of cultural objects enclosing a paper illustrating the interim measures for the return of works of art and other cultural objects taken by the Germans from the occupied territories approved by the RDR Division, dated December 1945. Also includes a list of three appendices to the paper providing examples of an inventory property card, a request card and a receipt form [not included in this piece]. Further correspondence between UK and US Deputy Military Governors Robertson and Clay, the I A and C Division and the British Embassy in Washington relating to the question of 'the disposal of German works of art captured during the battle phase of the recent operations' and requesting reassurance from Clay that 'those works of art which were removed from the British Zone either under orders of the SHAEF, or as the result of action taken by the Germans to move them to safer localities, will not be shipped to the United States but will be returned to the British Zone in the near future', dated October-November 1945. Cipher messages from the British Element of the Control Commission for Germany in Berlin to the Chief of Staff on the subject of the restitution of works of art, stamped October-November 1945. Records that no invitations had yet been sent to foreign experts to identify works of art as in Hamburg the work of separation of works of art had only just been completed, and that 785 bells had until that point been returned to Belgium while a further 300 Dutch bells had been identified and awaited shipment. Further states that the 'French have put forward a paper for quadripartite agreement of interim restitution of cultural works', whose definition was 'much wider than works of art'. Three copies of the agenda for the second meeting of the Cultural Works Committee of the RDR Directorate to be held on 22 October 1945. Copy of the Monthly Report No 1 of the Military Governor of the US Zone on Monuments, Fine Arts and Archives, dated August 1945. Includes a synopsis summarising the activity of the American MFA and A officers and their objectives: 'the protection and preservation of religious, artistic, historic or other similar cultural buildings or materials in Germany', 'the reactivation of German civilian administration concerned therewith', 'the restitution to their pre-war owners of cultural materials confiscated by the Nazis within Germany or looted by the Germans from territories occupied by them' and 'in so far as concerns archives, documents and records [.] the exploitation of such materials for immediate intelligence needs'. Includes a map illustrating the geographical distribution of art depositories in the US Zone and a graph with a quantification of the types of repositories discovered in the US Zone. Describes in detail the work of identification, supervision, packing and delivery of the cultural material kept in the repositories entrusted to the MFA and A officers. Letter from the Property Control branch of the Finance Division to the French section of the RDR Division, dated September referring any questions concerning art objects or archives to the authority of Col Webb of the MFA and A branch, dated September 1945. Extract from the minutes of the official Committee on Armistice Terms and Civil Administration held on 19 September 1945 recording the Committee's decisions with regard to the tasks and scope of the proposed German archives panel, as reported by the chairman of the Interdepartmental Political Working Party on Germany and Austria..

context: Records of Naval Staff Departments.
adminHistory: The Naval Staff divisions bear responsibility for the distribution and readiness of the Fleet and its effectiveness in the event of war. They are concerned with the framing of strategy and tactics, the planning and conduct of operations, and the collection and dissemination of intelligence. They operate under the First Sea Lord as Chief of Naval Staff, supported by a Vice-Chief of Naval Staff and Assistant Chiefs of Naval Staff. It is also their task to indicate to the responsible departments the needs of the Navy as regards manpower, training, weapons and materials. Through the First Sea Lord's membership of the Chiefs of Staff Committee and the service of the Vice-Chief of Naval Staff on the Deputy Chiefs of Staff Committee, links are maintained with the Army and Air Force. The institution of a formal Naval Staff within the Admiralty in 1912 arose from an evident need for plans to form the basis of a coherent naval strategy in the event of war and had been preceded by pressure to this end from the Committee of Imperial Defence and the appointment of Churchill as First Lord in 1911. Initially the Naval Staff had three divisions (dealing with operations, mobilisation and intelligence), but it was not until the end of the First World War, by which time it possessed twelve divisions, that it had an organisation suitable for its task. For an account of developments during this period see The Admiralty by Dr N A M Rodger (Terence Dalton Ltd, 1979). For information concerning Naval Staff organisation during the Second World War see John D. Cantwell, The Second World War: A Guide to Documents in the Public Record Office (PRO Handbooks, XV, 2nd edn, 1992), 17-28. Although the Naval Staff's divisional organisation changed from time to time, there was an Operations Division during both World Wars responsible for the operational control of ships with a separate Combined Operations Division, liaising with Combined Operations Headquarters, from 1943. There was also a Plans Division concerned with questions of strategy as well as operational plans and providing, during the Second World War, the naval part of the Joint Planning Staff. Another key division was the Trade Division, responsible for the protection of maritime trade and trooping by means of the organisation of convoys and escorts and by the fitting of armaments in merchant vessels. In this connection, it worked closely in both World Wars with the Ministries of Shipping and, from 1941, with the Ministry of War Transport. The division was also associated with the Economic Warfare Division, responsible for contraband control (in concert with the Ministry of Economic Warfare, and it had links with the Anti-Submarine Warfare Division, both these divisions also forming part of the Naval Staff. There was also a Naval Air Division, responsible for the policy and organisation of the Fleet Air Arm and, from 1944, a Signals Division created to deal with communications separately from the production of communications equipment, which remained in the Signal Department. A Local Defence Division was responsible for naval defences at home and abroad; the Minesweeping Division was separated from it shortly after the out-break of war in 1939. There was also a Training and Staff Duties Division, within which was included a Historical Section. A Gunnery and Anti-Aircraft Division was established in 1941. Also part of the Naval Staff was the Naval Intelligence Division. This had been formed in 1886 in succession to the Foreign Intelligence Committee, which had existed from 1882. It concerned itself not only with the collection of information about foreign navies, but also with war planning. In July 1917 it absorbed the small group of civilian experts engaged since the outbreak of the First World War on the deciphering of enemy naval wireless signals. This group was known as 'Room 40' after the room in which they were housed in the Old Admiralty Building. 'Room 40' became the core of the Government Code and Cipher School (GCCS) established on 1 November 1919, still under the control of the Director of Naval Intelligence, but intended to work for and with all government departments interested in wireless intelligence and cryptography. On l April 1922 control of the GCCS passed to the Foreign Office. During both the First and Second World Wars there was a Geographical Section attached to the Naval Intelligence Division responsible for producing handbooks on various parts of the world, dealing with geographical, geological, ethnological, historical, etc factors affecting the countries concerned, illustrated by maps, diagrams and photographs. In 1937 an Operational Intelligence Centre to serve the Naval Staff was established and it was to this centre that the naval section of the Government Code and Cipher School at Bletchley Park sent the deciphered texts of enemy signals during the Second World War. In 1940 the Topographical Section of the Naval Intelligence Division was evacuated to the School of Geography at Oxford. The urgent need for reports regarding areas in which combined operations or opposed landings might take place resulted in the expansion of the work of the section which became an organ of the Chiefs of Staffs Committee as the Inter-Services Topographical Department. The department came directly under the orders of that committee, but continued to be administered by the division. In 1963 the Naval Intelligence Division became part of the Joint Intelligence Staff, which soon afterwards came under the new Ministry of Defence.
description: This division contains regularly printed lists showing the disposition of vessels: 'Pink lists' are in ADM 187 , 'Red lists' in ADM 208 , 'Blue lists' in ADM 209 and 'Green lists' in ADM 210 The 'Wireless News' bulletin issued by the Naval Intelligence Division, later by the GCCS, 1918-21, is in ADM 233. Reports of the Foreign Intelligence Committee and the Naval Intelligence Division are in ADM 231. Intelligence reports and summaries of the Division and of the Operational Intelligence Centre during the Second World War and the immediate post-war period, and other miscellaneous records of the Division are in ADM 223 Convoy records are in ADM 237 and minelaying operations records in ADM 243.

description: Folio 106: Wickfort to [Williamson]. 'R[ecu] de la Haye du 5 mars de Wickfort. Les lettres de la semaine passé des ambassadeurs de cet état donnent un peu plus d'espérance que ne font leurs derniers, quoique je crois qu'ils surmonteront dans peu de temps toutes lesautres difficultés, puisqu'ils ont pu vaincre celle de la pêche. Il y a des provinces entières qui voudraient que le traité ne se fît point, à cause de l'aversion qu'[elles] ont pour ce garantie générale, en sorte que si elles trouvent occasion de le traverser elles le feront, ce qui est très sûr. Il n'y personne ici qui ne demeure d'accord que les trois colonels anglais ne meritent les derniers et plus cruels supplices, mais comme on est ici dans un état fort libre, on voudrait que capture se fût fait dans les formes; le roi d'Angleterre est tellement satisfait du procède des Etats Généraux en cette rencontre qu'il en a remercié les ambassadeurs de bouche et a dit qu'il le ferait encore écrit en écrivant tant aux Etats Généraux qu'aux particulières de cette province. Je crois que cela aidera à l'avancement du traité si ce n'est que le roi se trouve offensé de la guarantie de la pêche que l'on a demandée et obtenue de la France. Estévan de Gamare est ici depuis quatre ou cinq jours. Il ne parlera pas de l'alliance défensive qu'il voulait faire la proposition parce qu'il est très certain qu'il [ne] réussira pas. Il a dit que le roi, son maître, lui a écrit que s'il était à Bruxelles, qu'il y demeura, et que s'il était en Angleterre, il fit entendre au roi que son maître voulait qu'il allât en Hollande pour son service, qu'il en avait usé ainsi parce qu'il ne voulait pas que son ambassadeur fût presenté a l'entrée de la reine, ni qu'il la complimenta. L'ambassadeur de Portugal fit savoir lundi à Messieurs les Etats Généraux que le roi son maître a revoqué toutes les commissions qu'il a données contre les habitants de ces provinces et qu'il a défendu tous actes d'hostilité. Il a dit qu'il aura la ratification du traité dans 15 jours. Il y a grand intérêt à la faire venir parce qu'il n'aura pas d'audience qu'il ne l'aît délivrée et l'on n'entera pas en conférence avec lui. Quand la cour de France verra qu'il n'y aura rien a faire en Pologne, elle ne se soucier guère de l'amitie de Monsieur l'Electeur. Il y a grande apparance que l'on contentera l'armée et qu'après cela on fera la paix avec les Moscovites, mais on ne serait plus parler de l'élection d'un successeur pendant la vie du roi Il y a des gens qui rendent de fort mauvais offices au roi de Pologne?. Date and place: 1662 Mar 5 Hague.

description: "The last letter I received from you was of the 14th of December, and though I concur with our best friend's [Cecil's] desire and yours to have you go for England, yet I cannot but be glad of your resolution to settle that province, which I hope may be now speedily done since you are rid of that rogue Tirrell. But since the occasion that is prescribed me to send you over must be to deliver the full estate of this country upon some consultation held by the Council, I think it will be necessary that you do meet me at Dublin. The way I do leave to yourself, and the time, since the public respect doth sway with your private desire. "I do think I shall hardly go any further than this place, since I have intended a course utterly to ruin O'Rurke, who is the only lord that in all Ulster, Leinster, or Connaught doth at this time remain in rebellion, except such as are beaten out of their countries, for McGuire, that was the last, is clean driven out of his country, and is now with O'Rurke. They both do sue for peace, but O'Rurke in a more proud fashion than stands with the honour of the Estate to hearken unto him. For Tirrell, although he may chance to burn or spoil some rotten houses and little better subjects, yet I doubt but by the grace of God I shall soon take some order with his worship. "Here I cannot stay long, and farther now I cannot well go; yet I would fain speak with you, for the Queen hath absolutely commanded that I shall present[ly] reduce the list unto twelve thousand foot and unto a thousand horse, so that according to your proportion the cast must fall also upon your companies; about the which I would willingly confer with you. And this far I am come only to that purpose, for now my business doth only lie about Alone, whither if from Lymricke you can send any store of victuals, you shall exceedingly advance the service. We are all, as much as we may, to help one another; but they say here that you owe to this province a great deal of victuals which you stayed at Cork, being directed hither. But, howsoever, what you can possibly spare I pray take order that it be sent to Athlone, for from Galloway we cannot possibly send any great quantity thither. "I hope my letter will find you about Lymrick, for long since I have written to you my resolution to be here at this time; and the more haste you make hither the more glad I shall be, for I would fain return speedily, and shortly I must of necessity." From Galloway, 24 December. P.S.--"Presently after Christmas there do come Commissioners out of England about many matters. It will be exceeding good that you should be there then, and to carry into England the report of the success." Addressed. Endorsed: Received 26 December 1602, at Limerick. The words in italics are in cipher, mostly deciphered by Carew.
title: LORD DEPUTY MOUNTJOY to SIR GEORGE CAREW.

context: Manuscripts.Carew Manuscript.
description: "The last I wrote was of the escape of Cormocke McDermod. The ties which I have upon him are such, as he is a suitor to be reconciled to the State. My answers are, if he will justify himself of his accusations as a good subject ought to do (and which he may safely do if he be innocent), he shall have a just trial. If he dare not stand upon his innocency, then I will him to confess his errors, and he be an humble suitor for her Majesty's gracious pardon, who rather desireth amendment of life in offenders than their extirpation. Which if he do, and submit himself to such assurances as the State shall think meet to require of him, I will then be a suitor to your Lordship for a remission of all his offences. What his answer will be, I do not yet know, but hourly expect. Whatsoever it is, I know he can do no great hurt, for already he is little better than a banished man out of his country of Muskerry, for I have in the same all the principal castles that command the country. His chiefest followers, with all their creaghts, I have disposed upon assurances under the Lord Roche, the Lord Barry, Sir John FitzEdmonds, and Sir Walter Raleghe's signory. Besides, I have a strong faction of his nearest kinsmen against him, and his eldest son is in England, and his wife and his two eldest daughters in Cork, so as none but the looser sort follow him, who, when his subjection seemed to be most secured to the State, were evermore purposely by him left with the traitors, whom, as he would allege, he could not rule. Wherefore, if your Lordship have any occasion to employ the forces here above the list of Munster, you may dispose them as your Lordship shall think best, but until such occasion be ministered their abode here will do me no hurt. "This day I received a letter from your Lordship, signifying your pleasure unto me that you had appointed one Hussie to be sheriff of the county of Kerry. Sir George Bourchier therein hath prevented my suit, for I thought to have been an humble suitor to your Lordship that all the sheriffs of Munster might stand as they did for one year longer. The reasons that leads me unto it is the sufficiencies I find in them; and although it be against the ordinary course of law that sheriffs should remain above one year in their office, yet in turbulent times when a good officer is made that serves her Majesty with diligence and without exclamation of the country (under your Lordship's correction), I think it no error to continue him. I protest.. there is not a sheriff in this province that hath made suit unto me to be continued in his place more than one, which is John Barry, sheriff of the county of Cork, and him of all others I do most earnestly sue for, being an active man in his disposition in this turbulent time. He is the best struggling officer in effecting the commandments that are laid upon him that ever I saw, whereas one of a weaker spirit and less ability to execute his place could bear only the name and not the power of a sheriff. I am sure by him, without aid of soldiers, to have my directions performed, which by others, if he were displaced, I could not expect. Besides, since his company is taken from him, it is not ill counsel to hold him assured to the State. The rest of the sheriffs never made suit for their continuance, but finding them honest and not complained upon, I do think it were not amiss to keep good officers in their places. Nevertheless, if your Lordship be not so pleased, I will send you a list hereinclosed of fit men in every shire, Cork and Kerry excepted; the one which I humbly entreat for John Barry, the other already bestowed upon Hussie, one of the same country; and so in all counties in my opinion is the best election. "I did promise to send your Lordship a book of all Cormock's treasons, which is in writing and not yet finished. If ever your Lordship in so short time saw more, or more foul ones, committed by any man, I am deceived. And although.. he is escaped, yet I doubt not your Lordship will not only allow and approve his apprehension, but rather blame the Council here and me for letting him run so long time as he did unrestrained. By the next your Lordship shall have the book sent unto you. "Touching the Baron of Parliament, [In the margin: "The Lord Caher."] of whom your Lordship and the Council wrate unto me, your directions shall be obeyed. Sir George Thornton is landed, and before him by one day the Earl of Thomond. All the supplies are not yet arrived. Of those which came with Sir George, I have delivered 200 of them unto Sir Edward Wingfeld. The long sword may light upon whom the destiny is assigned. Of his being hurt by Captain Francis Kingsmyll I am sure your Lordship hath heard. At the first the wound was but light, but by what accident or disorder I know not, it is proved dangerous at the least to the loss of the use of his leg, if not of his life, for he swells into the body, for diversion whereof the surgeons are fain to make issues both in his leg under his knee and under his buttock; I am verily persuaded that he will hardly ever hereafter recover the use of that limb. The wound was in his flank, of no great depth, and over-hastily healed, which breeeds him the dangers he is in. "By this intelligence enclosed it appears that the Spaniards come not this winter, and that O'Donnell is dead, whereof your Lordship may be assured, for the merchants that bringeth me the news I do trust, and I do think it will fall out that he is poisoned [The words in italics are in cipher, undeciphered.] by James Blake, of whom your Lordship hath been formerly acquainted. At his coming into Spain he was suspected by O'Donnell, because he embarked at Corke, ["Coade" in MS., but evidently a mistake for "Corke." There are many similar errors in Carew's ciphered despatches.] but afterward he insinuated his access, and O'Donnell is dead. He never told the President in what manner he would kill him, but did assure him it should be effected. It will not be many days before the truth will appear." Cork, 9 October 1602. P.S.--"Since the writing hereof I received a submissive letter from Cormock McDermod. He desires the Queen's pardon, and refuseth justification. I have granted him to speak with me here." Copy.
title: SIR G. CAREW to LORD DEPUTY MOUNTJOY.

context: Local Government Board and predecessors: Correspondence with Poor Law Unions and Other Local Authorities. Nottinghamshire Poor Law Unions. Mansfield 337. Mansfield 337. (Described at item level).
description: Content: Folios 189-190. Letter from E Gulson, Assistant Poor Law Commissioner, to the Poor Law Commission, enclosing a letter from Mr Coke, [not included] to show the state of matters in Mansfield. He states that the hand bill [not included] is what might be expected for the mob was all powerful and the document is drawn up so as to keep favour with that class. Gulson states that it is necessary for strong measures to be taken to enforce the Commission's authority. There are good guardians at the board but there are others whose conduct produces bad results, particularly the overseer and guardian of Mansfield. He is a large manufacturer who has been entrusted with the manufacturing scheme on the part of the board. His conduct at the conference with the delegation was inappropriate, calling the board of guardians 'mere ciphers' and telling the men, that the Commission did as they pleased, that it was no use troubling the guardians. These observations made to Mr Gulson at the board are, as Mr Coke in his letter states, to have been repeated. He believes that firm and resolute determination and a power on hand to keep the peace are needed as the board is divided, presided over by Mr Unwin whose conduct has been adverted to and who said 'that the Commissioners had lief do the work themselves', and the magistrates are on such bad terms that they do not speak or sit together. The union accounts are in great confusion, with no account kept of the work done by the poor of each parish or of the goods manufactured by the paupers of each parish, except in one general account which is kept by the guardian and overseer of Mansfield who is employing his own servants in giving out and taking in work. Despite instructions from Gulson and the Commission, the guardians have again resolved to continue the stocking making for another week, indicating to the boisterous and turbulent workpeople that they are not firm and that the authority of the Commission may be infringed. The workmen are paid in such a manner as to make the pauper best off and thus offer a premium to the men to come to the overseers instead of striving to otherwise maintain themselves. Gulson thinks that good men like Coke are driven from the board and the hostile guardians are predominant. As a result the union officers have no confidence and act without authority or uniformity. There is an election taking place in the county and Mansfield is the polling place and Gulson intends to be away that day. He suggests that a letter is written to the overseers of Mansfield directing them not to employ the people in stocking making. A force either civil or military ought to be sent to the town to uphold the authority of the Commission, as want of firmness on the part of the board of guardians is ruinous to all order and principle of action. The schism between the magistrates prevents them stepping in to assist with any degree of vigour. The letter from the clerk, Mr Gulson believes, was drawn up by Mr Unwin. He asks for advice on what is best to be done. He will to go to Mansfield on Thursday if that is the wish of the Commission but it will be a riotous polling day. Annotated: return Mr Coke's letter. See 6292/C/1849. Paper Number: 6389/C/1837. Poor Law Union Number 337. Counties: Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire.
